subtopic: MR. LAING-DISTRIBUTION OF BILL AMENDING PRESENT LEGISLATION

speakeroldname: Hon. Arlhur Laing (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: MR. LAING-DISTRIBUTION OF BILL AMENDING PRESENT LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Yesterday the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Yukon asked me whether in fact a distribution had been made to the council of the Northwest Territories, now in session in Ottawa, of a bill, then in draft form, to amend the Northwest Territories Act. My reply was that I would be extremely surprised if this proved to be the case.
I have to acknowledge that I have been more than extremely surprised, and that distribution was made. I think there may be some small extenuating circumstance in the fact that the bill contains provisions which in effect involve amendments to the constitution of the Northwest Territories, but I would ask no consideration of the house on this basis. I make an apology to the house for this distribution, and I assure hon. members that this sort of thing will not happen again.

subtopic: MR. LAING-DISTRIBUTION OF BILL AMENDING PRESENT LEGISLATION
speechtext:
On the question of privilege may I simply say that it is always desirable to make the fullest possible
information available to the members of the councils of both territories, a practice which has been followed only too infrequently in the past. However, in this case a distribution was made prematurely. It may even be that the hon. member for the Northwest Territories might have knowledge of the bill. I make no suggestion that he does, but the possibility is ever present.
In the circumstances, and because of the circulation which the bill has received, I think the minister or the Prime Minister or the leader of the house might give hon. members an assurance that this legislation will now be introduced and tabled at the earliest possible moment so that all in this house might have the same information that has been made available to others, because after all it is a federal statute that we are concerned with.
AUTOMOTIVE PARTS-LOSS OF CONTRACTS BY CANADIAN STAMPING COMPANIES On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Finance and ask him whether the government has received complaints from officials of some 70 Canadian stamping companies relating to the lack of opportunity for Canadian firms to bid on the supply of automobile parts for this year's production, and also whether he has reason to believe that the automobile companies-the big three-are not giving Canadians the right to bid but are in fact transferring this work to American companies in the United States.
What is the government's position in this regard? Will the minister do what he can to assure that the big three, who benefit so greatly from this agreement, will have it made clear to them that Canadian companies should have the opportunity to retain what has been described as millions of dollars worth of contracts as has been the case in the past?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have received representations from the automobile parts manufacturers along the lines outlined by the Leader of the Opposition. These representations related to my

January 25, 1966
Inquiries of the Ministry portfolio in so far as they would affect the budget. They were among the representations made to me by a large number of people and organizations relating to the budget itself and, as usual, I have promised them the most careful consideration.

Is this a proper assessment of the situation, and will the minister tell us whether millions of dollars of business will be lost to these Canadian companies. speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of Industry):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the house will be aware that there is a resolution on the order paper which will provide a better opportunity than orders of the day for a complete discussion of this question. As a further supplementary question may I ask the minister whether his department is taking any action in order to assure itself and the country that there will be no large scale loss of orders for metal stamping in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can give the hon. member that assurance. No one is more concerned than the Department of Industry that the very substantial expansion which is taking place in the automobile manufacturing sector in Canada shall be accomplished with a minimum of dislocation and a minimum of hardship, and daily we are directing all our efforts toward that end.
Inevitably, in a process of change, a process of expansion, there will be some hardship, but it is our intention to keep it to a minimum.

the committees, such as banking and commerce, to enable the members of the house to get all the facts, or as many facts as possible, on this whole matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would hope this would come before the house at the earliest possible opportunity.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the
January 25. 1966	COMMONS
Minister of Labour in his capacity in charge of the administration of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I realize it also concerns the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources and the Minister of Finance. In view of the announcement that the interest rate on Central Mortgage and Housing loans in the Northwest Territories is now to be 7f per cent, 1 per cent over the new rate recently announced for mortgages elsewhere in Canada, does the minister think the government is encouraging the development of the north by penalizing investors for investing in the Northwest Territories; and is it an equitable policy to raise the interest cost above the 60th parallel as compared with below that parallel?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES-INTEREST RATE ON C.M.H.C. LOANS
speechtext: Order. It seems to me that at this time the hon. member is asking for an expression of opinion.

subtopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES-INTEREST RATE ON C.M.H.C. LOANS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with respect to your ruling with regard to my question, I should like to re-ask the Minister of Labour whether it is government policy to insist on a higher rate of interest for central housing and mortgage loans in the Northwest Territories.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES-INTEREST RATE ON C.M.H.C. LOANS
speechtext:
I am very glad that the hon. member has put his question a second time, because this enables me to assure the house that the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation does not have two rates.
There are in fact three types of loans in the Yukon. The first is the normal N.H.A. loan made by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. In that case, the interest rate is 6f per cent, the same as it is in all parts of Canada. I understand, however, that there are second mortgage loans made by the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, on which the maximum is $2,000. The rate in such cases has usually been 1 per cent higher than the rate on central mortgage loans.
There is a third type of first mortgage loan, Mr. Speaker, a loan up to $6,000, together with special grants if the occupant lives in the house for a period of ten years, I believe it is. He then benefits from a forgiveness provision. In that case I believe the rate is also 71 per cent. The N.H.A. rate for all hemes in Canada is uniform, both in the territories as well as the provinces.

subtopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES-INTEREST RATE ON C.M.H.C. LOANS
speechtext:

Mr. Speaker, I should like to join with those who have spoken before me in extending to you, sir, my sincere congratulations on your election, which was unanimous, as Speaker of the house.
Your past experience and the manner in which you have discharged your responsibilities as Acting Speaker leave no doubt as to your great ability and qualifications, even if this task is often most delicate. I should also like to take this opportunity to congratulate the Acting Speaker and chairman of committees and, also, to extend congratulations to the hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Goyer) and the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury) who have moved and seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They did it with dignity and I am sure that the whole country will benefit by the knowledge and talent they bring to this house.
The speech from the throne, Mr. Speaker, is right to the point and the program outlined for the first session of the twenty seventh par-
January 25, 1966

The Address-Mr. Matte liament could help, through the work of all its members, to maintain the growth of our beautiful Canada for the greater good of all Canadians. In addition, it will bring a ray of hope to the needy through the war on poverty already started under a Liberal government, and the speech from the throne confirms this fact.
This brings me to deal first with the economic poverty to be found within certain classes in this country; second, with the duty of government and all individuals to cope, first of all, with this serious problem; third, what has been done by the new Liberal government; and fourth, what it proposes to do in this state of war.
Although some define poverty as a purely relative fact, depending on the place and the era, to me it is the state of those who are deprived of what they need to live and to play a citizen's role in society.
Most Canadians will agree that no citizen in this country should be, through outside causes, deprived from the benefits of modern civilization. It is our social responsibility to give everybody an opportunity to enjoy a certain degree of comfort.
A great philosopher, reflecting on poverty, has concluded that a modicum of welfare is required to fulfil properly one's religious and, consequently, one's civic duties.
Although all citizens must be considered equal in the eyes of the law, a poor person's shortcomings are always more excusable. A minimum of welfare will make a man a better citizen or simply a true Canadian.
The report on rural poverty in four regions prepared and published for ARDA by the Canadian welfare council in Ottawa should give us food for thought. The discoveries made in these four countries are true, to a varying degree, of almost all the rural and urban regions of the country.
I should like to give you a summary of these conditions as seen by community leaders and by the poor families whose conception of poverty is entirely different.
The former see poverty in its overall aspect, that is, its causes and effects; in other words, they grasp the concept better. The latter define it rather in terms of their own situation and that of their neighbour.
The definition given by community leaders generally bears a close resemblance to the reasons set forth during the case survey. Here are, in order of importance, the common factors most often included by those community leaders in such a definition:

Economic poverty: lack of personal income, too heavy family responsibilities, uneconomic land or farm, chronic unemployment, jobs that do not pay enough or are hard to get.
Personal or family deficiencies: inadequate schooling of children and parents, illness, poor adaptation, irresponsibility, alcoholism, lack of social participation, slums, dire poverty, debts, mentally deficient children and parents, anxiety concerning the future, little opportunity for betterment, unfulfilled desire to improve, laziness, a single trade, old age.
Social deficiencies: unemployment, insufficient school and sanitary equipment, lack of recreational organizations (especially for the young), lack of social cohesion.
The concept of poverty in the family stresses above all the difficulties it experiences: "We are not earning enough to make ends meet", "It's tough going", "We don't know what we will eat to-morrow". Elsewhere, frustrated ambition is more obvious: "We can't give our children any education", "We can't live like others do". The lack of essentials is illustrated in the two following definitions:	"To be poor is to wash your
clothes without soap" and "It is not to have any newspaper with which to light the stove."
Certain moral causes of poverty are expressed as follows: "He is poor because he is too lazy to work." "If So-and-So is poor, it is because he drinks too much; he often goes to the hotel". And then inadequacy steps in to explain poverty; for some "Poverty is lack of education" or "It is lack of intelligence."
Well, that is poverty. And that is what we find too often when we visit our ridings and when our electors pay us a visit.
According to the report from which I have just quoted, it was found that out of 63 families visited, 40 did not earn $50 per week. There were also too many poor families among our agricultural classes. After having made surveys, experts came to the conclusion that a family must earn at least $3,000 per year to be able to survive. According to the 1961 census, 23 per cent of Canadian families did not earn that amount. That is why it seems illogical to set at $2,000 a year the basic deduction for a family.
Poverty can easily prevent an individual from being a good citizen.
Therefore, a tremendous responsibility lies with our governments which must strive for the good of every citizen and particularly of those who are most in need.
January 25, 1966	COMMONS
The object of every piece of legislation must be to wage the great battle against poverty-I am not talking about class struggle-which must be eliminated before it is too late by bending every effort to ensure a higher degree of social justice.
It is very well to make surveys, but action is also needed. I, therefore, commend the government which has not only tackled this problem unceasingly but has intensified the fight in recent years. The government has even created the Department of Rural Development which has already accomplished a great deal and which will carry on the good work, I am sure, to the benefit of all citizens across Canada. I should also like to stress the importance of the federal-provincial conference on poverty held last December 7-10, to find solutions to existing problems.
We would have everything to gain by refraining from wasting precious time in seeking sensationalism or trying to find fault with others and by spending more time on dealing with real problems; in short, let us not fight constitutional battles when stark poverty is the order of the day.
It is not all to propose old age pensions of $100 and family allowances of $25. Why not $150 or $200 for our old people and $40 or more for every child? I should like it myself as well as all the other members, but appropriate means must be found to balance the budget and deal with the other problems: health, education, welfare. However, nobody wants higher taxes and there is no adequate dollar factory. Nevertheless, it is the Liberal government which established pensions, allowances and implemented many other pieces of legislation to help the needy and it is always ready to do more when possible.
Mr. Speaker, in reviewing carefully the speech from the throne, we find that the present government wants to keep on waging an intense fight against poverty. Most measures proposed are big guns ready to fire in this fight.
Of the main points of the legislative program, at least 75 per cent are aimed more or less directly at poverty among individuals, farmers, and rural and urban groups. In addition to the establishment of a Department of Manpower, the following measures are proposed: increased assistance to universities and scholarship plans; a measure to establish a Canadian health insurance plan after consultation with the provinces-with which I agree; the establishment of a $500 million health fund; the establishment of a

When Charles Dickens viewed the opening of parliament in Nova Scotia in 1842 he wrote down his impressions as follows:
It was like looking at Westminster through the wrong end of the telescope. The Governor delivered the Speech from the Throne. The military band outside struck up God Save The Queen with great vigour; the people shouted; the 'ins' rubbed their hands, the 'outs' shook their heads, the government party said there never was such a good speech; the opposition declared there never was such a bad one; and in short, everything went on, and promised to go on, just as it does at home.
I believe Dickens' observations aptly describe the opening of the twenty seventh parliament, and the Throne Speech introduced by the present minority Liberal administration. This Throne Speech would indicate that the present Liberal government is, to paraphrase Dickens, still looking at some of the problems of the Atlantic provinces through the wrong end of a telescope. This makes them look small, inconsequential and far away when in fact they are very large and of significant importance to the Atlantic region of the nation, and they must be dealt with now if the people of the Atlantic provinces are to rise above the income disparities and lack of employment opportunities that have plagued this area for decades.
Since the recent election members of the Liberal party, meeting in secret and in caucus, have done much soul searching in an attempt to analyse the reasons for their overall loss of federal seats in the Atlantic provinces. When you look at the small number of Liberals elected in Nova Scotia this is understandable. No doubt the party sages have developed some acceptable alibis, but in my opinion the underlying factor leading to the Liberal route in Nova Scotia is the general mistrust by the majority of citizens of the Liberal party and its promises.

I hope the situation remains such, and that we will be able to come back in September and finish the work we have on the agenda for this session.

But what happened? Regenstreif, Gallup and the Liberal go-go boys convinced the Prime Minister that it was politically expedient to call an election in November. "We can win 143 seats," they told him, "so let's go-go. What is $14 or $15 million of the taxpayers' money, if we can get a majority?" Now, with a billion dollars in promises to be fulfilled after the election, the Grits are almost right back where they started from, but not quite. Some of the go-go boys are gone, but the false advice followed by the immature action of the Liberal party and its leaders will long be remembered by many Canadians.
I could go on much longer in a critical way about the political opportunists who presently occupy the government benches, but I believe that five federal elections in eight years, with four of them returning minority governments, have given politics priority over programs too much of the time. There is a mass of unfinished business awaiting government action, and the manner in which this is handled will make the twenty seventh parliament a pride or a disappointment.
"Well," you may say, "where shall we begin?" Speaking as a Nova Scotian I believe that province, which played a major role in founding Canada, has a right to share in the growth and prosperity of this nation. Speaking as a Canadian I would not ask for policies that would be harmful to Canada. However, I know you will agree it is discouraging to learn that in 1966 the amount of money the average man in the Atlantic provinces takes home in pay is almost a third less than that of his equivalent elsewhere in Canada. And this is the position after ten years of enterprise, a period in which we have seen the establishment of a self-help group called the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council, the Atlantic Development Board, the New Brunswick Development Corporation, Industrial Estates in Nova Scotia, the Department of Economic Development in Newfoundland, and other government agencies designed to encourage economic growth.
You may well ask what are the results of this effort, for in Halifax, Dartmouth and throughout parts of Nova Scotia new industries are opening up. Well, the answer is that there has been some improvement. In 1956 the income per head in the Atlantic provinces was 65 per cent of the Canadian average, while in 1964 it was 68.4 per cent. This is an improvement of 3.4 per cent, just a tenth of the gap. Now we have to close the balance of the gap, and it is a huge task.

We need more secondary industries, but we do not want new industries that require continuing support. In addition to secondary industries we need massive investment by the federal government. But Nova Scotia and its people can depend only on itself and the federal government for the development necessary to put it in line with the rest of Canada. Therefore a strong central government is necessary if the country is to progress uniformly. I believe it is of the greatest importance to Nova Scotia that the national government have sufficient authority to take the lead in developing Canada as a whole, and I express the hope that this government will take steps to prevent any further erosion of federal powers.
It is not easy for a province like Nova Scotia to catch up with the rest of Canada in material wealth. According to the second annual review of the Economic Council of Canada the per capita income in Nova Scotia was three quarters of the Canadian average. Even to hold our own we have to make the same percentage gains as the rest of Canada. To reduce the gap we have to make greater gains than the rest of Canada. To do this we need the active co-operation of the government of Canada.
One area of assistance that would be helpful to Nova Scotia would be the inclusion of the required expansion of our tourist accommodation and facilities under the incentive grants program as set out in Bill No. C-129. The tourist industry is vitally important to Nova Scotia, and the manner in which this industry is growing is indicated by the fact that our tourist figures for 1965 show that our province had 900,000 visitors as compared with our resident population of 762,000. This many tourists bring an estimated $58 million to $60 million to our province. The further
The Address-Mr. Crouse expansion of this industry is primarily dependent on the change in the federal definition of the act. I believe that changes could be made under clauses 2 (d) and (e). Clause 2(d) reads:
"development grant" means a grant under this act by way of assistance for the establishment of a new facility or the expansion of an existing facility in the designated area;
Then clause 2(e) reads:
"facility" means the structures, machinery and equipment that constitute the necessary components of a manufacturing or processing operation:
Under this new interpretation the policy of recognizing the tourist industry for incentive grants would not only be helpful to Nova Scotia but would become the policy for all Canada.
In fact the federal government has now a golden opportunity to provide Nova Scotia with the funds urgently required for the necessary expansion of our tourist facilities. I can think of no policy change, Mr. Speaker, that would be more helpful, especially in areas where there is no other industry, and I hope the government and the minister will give serious thought to this policy change which would be so helpful not only to the economy of all the Atlantic provinces but to the economy of all Canada.
Almost at the very end of the Throne Speech we were told that other legislative proposals would be placed before us, including amendments to the Atlantic Development Board Act. I would like to suggest that this legislation be placed a little closer to the top of the government's list of priorities so that an early start can be made on the harnessing of the Fundy tides. Power to turn the wheels of industry is needed in ever increasing amounts in Nova Scotia, and it has been estimated that the Bay of Fundy has a potential annual power capacity in excess of 9 million horsepower. This power development is of prime concern to our province. For over 50 years the minds of men have contemplated the idea of harnessing this great natural force to produce electric power. However, the cost of development, plus the problem of transporting this power to distant markets discouraged serious consideration of this project.
I was very pleased today to hear the Minister of Transport state in answer to a question that the matter of setting up a committee to study this project is now under active consideration. Today, modern earth-moving equipment makes the huge dams
222	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Crouse possible and modern technological and engineering advances have virtually solved the power transportation problem. The Atlantic Development Board has already done some work in this field, reviewing the material gathered to date on this subject. However, speed is of the essence, for if reliable estimates of costs and production are not gained soon, other methods of generating electricity via atomic energy may well be developed to the point where tidal generation will be economically unattractive.
Three projects are feasable; one at Shepody Bay, one at Cumberland Basin and one at Minas Basin. The construction of a dam between Cape Split and Parrsboro in Minas Basin would not only increase Nova Scotia's power potential but would also provide immense side benefits in terms of improved road transport and recreation areas. Here I should add, Mr. Speaker, that the development of this power would not only attract new industries to Nova Scotia but would also be helpful to New Brunswick, where the rapid growth of the mining, smelting, chemical, fuel and paper industries has created an unprecedented demand for electric power in recent years.
I am sure that all Canadians welcomed the announcement of increased aid to our universities as contained in the Throne Speech. In Nova Scotia we agree with the report of the Economic Council of Canada that education is a crucially important factor contributing to economic growth and rising living standards. This will enable our universities to continue to provide an educational service for all of Canada. Our universities educate as many outsiders as natives, and while no one objects to this service being performed, it is one of the major reasons why our universities face a financial crisis, e (12:30 p.m.)
A generous federal policy toward higher education in the Atlantic provinces can be supported for national as well as regional reasons. However, in my opinion, the announced increase in per capita grants is just the beginning of the increased federal support that will be needed if provincial governments are to carry out the university expansion programs to which they are committed.
Serving as I do as one of the governors on the board of Waterloo Lutheran University, I am well aware of the capital funds that are required for expansion, not only of that university but of all universities throughout Canada. At the present time over $500 million

DEBATES	January 25, 1966
is pledged in contracts for expansion of Canadian universities, and construction is at various stages. No one will deny the necessity for this expansion, but looking forward some ten years it seems to me the government will have to initiate discussions on all aspects of university financing, especially if they are to have sufficient funds for capital programs and research.
I suggest also that the government give serious consideration to the Bladen commission recommendation that the present limit on gifts to universities that may be deducted from income and corporate taxes be revised upward. An amendment to the Income Tax Act to accommodate larger gifts to universities would encourage greater support from private citizens as well as corporations.
The Speech from the Throne states:
My government will continue to strengthen the capacity of the integrated Canadian Defence Forces to provide for the security of Canada and to contribute abroad to the preservation of peace. Amendments to the National Defence Act will be laid before you.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I propose that the amendments call for the establishment of a Canada wide forest firefighting force. Large provinces with big populations and substantial financial resources like Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia can afford to employ fleets of water bombers and spotter planes to patrol and fight fires over their vast forests. However, in the smaller and poorer Atlantic provinces it is quite a different matter.
Nova Scotia, whose economy depends heavily on its forest resources, can afford to maintain only three spotter aircraft and one small water bomber. During the summer months, during the height of our province's forest fire season, we have to look around desperately for additional aircraft. What has been so galling to Nova Scotians watching the palls of black smoke rise above our valuable forest land while provincial firefighters struggle to control the spread of the fire, has been the fact that R.C.A.F. and Royal Canadian Navy aircraft have been standing by at military airfields in the province or engaging in routine patrols of less apparent urgency. In the past, requests for aid have generally met with the official reply that air force and naval aircraft are not equipped for water bombing, and that pilots and crews are not trained for this dangerous work.
This was the same argument that was advanced by the navy when a coast guard service was proposed. However, today this service, pro-
January 25, 1966

vided by the federal government through the Department of Transport and other integrated departments, is saving valuable shipping and the lives of Canadian seamen whenever disaster strikes. In my opinion a special wing of the R.C.A.F. should be formed, equipped, trained and made instantly ready for work in sny part of Canada where fires are destroying valuable forests, threatening the homes and lives of citizens and wildlife, while at the same time limiting the recreation areas which are an attraction for tourists as well as useful to our citizens.
The Speech from the Throne, which I consider the government's list of good intentions, stated that we would be asked to approve legislation to improve the movement and marketing of feed grain in eastern Canada and British Columbia by creating a livestock feed agency. The establishment of this agency will be watched with interest by the farmers in Nova Scotia, because the availability of feed grain at reasonable prices is vital to some lines of agriculture in our province, especially to those engaged in raising poultry and hogs. The annual bill for feed grain throughout the province is estimated in excess of $6 million. The census figures show that over the last 40 years Nova Scotia has become less and less dependent on its own feed resources. Between 1921 and 1961 wheat acreage shrank from 12,000 to 1,000 acres, while in the same period the acreage of oats shrank from 103,000 acres to 37,000 acres. I quote these figures to show that the province has never been more dependent on western grain than it is at the moment.
While this dependence continues there can be no serious thought of eliminating the present freight assistance policy. At the same time both agriculture and the government have every reason to be interested in the possibility of increasing local production. Every ton of grain produced locally will tend to decrease the cost of the freight assistance policy, and this fact alone would justify some government expenditure to encourage local production.
The federation of agriculture has asked for a subsidy of $8 per ton on locally grown grain. I believe such a request deserves careful consideration. Grain growing requires suitable land and capital. Of the two, capital is the most critical consideration in Nova Scotia. Capital is required for obtaining or opening up additional acreage, and even for temporary investment in fertilizer and feed grain. The subsidy proposed would, in the
The Address-Mr. Crouse words of the Minister of Finance add to the traditional means of fighting poverty. It would provide aid to those who are willing to work in order to improve their own position. It would make a worth-while contribution to the extra capital needs which Nova Scotia farmers require for a major expansion in grain production.
Even if this program were implemented we would still require improvements in the movement of western feed grains to Nova Scotia. This 24 year old federal policy has been based in part on the subsidized shipment of grain by sea, to Halifax, where it is stored and eventually distributed to Nova Scotia farmers. The trouble is that Halifax can only store about 50 per cent of the farmers' feed grain needs. It is evident we need more storage depots throughout the province, and I suggest that the government give serious thought to building grain storage facilities in Bridgewater, in Lunenburg county, which is in the heart of the farm community of both Lunenburg and Queens counties. This depot could serve the entire south shore, and distribution from this point could be administered by the new federal agency.
Following closely on the heels of the feed agency suggested in the Throne Speech, we read that a measure will be proposed for the development of the commercial fisheries of Canada. It is stated that we will be asked also to consider a proposal for income support for inshore fishermen in years of catch failure. These are stirring words for the inshore fisherman whose income is low because he is unable to catch and market the usual run of cod, haddock, halibut, pollock, hake, flounders or lobsters.
While any assistance to the fishing industry of the Atlantic provinces will be most welcome, I believe the fishermen would have preferred another type of announcement. This announcement could have been to this effect: "My government will recommend to parliament further measures calculated to give effect to Bill No. S-17, an act respecting the territorial sea and fishing zones of Canada, which parliament passed in 1964. Our object must be, without undue delay, to protect Canada's fisheries for Canadian fishermen."
This is the statement which should have appeared in the Throne Speech. By drawing base lines from geographical co-ordinates and thereby sealing off the Bay of Fundy and the Gulf of St. Lawrence as Canadian territorial waters, we would secure for our inshore
224	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Crouse fishermen protected areas and spawning areas that would gradually improve their catch and their income. But when questions are asked about the establishment of this 12 mile limit, either the Secretary of State for External Affairs or the Minister of Fisheries can only reply that these base lines are under negotiation.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
I believe the minister and his department would go a long way toward increasing the income of the average fisherman by assisting him to secure markets for the tons of fish which he is catching at present and throwing back into the sea as unsaleable. Here I refer to monkfish, skate, dogfish, sharks and mussels which are available in abundance to both our inshore and our offshore fishermen. Other countries have found a commercial value in these species and actively pursue the catching and marketing of them. Why cannot we do the same thing? Perhaps the fisheries minister could enlist the assistance of the Minister of Trade and Commerce who, through his trade representatives around the world, could ascertain the potential markets for these fish that are presently unmarketed.
Experiments conducted this year by the Nova Scotia fisheries development department indicate that both shrimp and crabs may be harvested from the Atlantic in commercial quantities. The Atlantic deep sea crab is found in waters from Greenland to Maine, and some are now being taken by a vessel operating out of Cheticamp, Cape Breton Island. It is similar to the heavily marketed king crab of the Pacific coast, and when mature has a body shell of five inches with legs ranging to ten inches in length. Since many of these shrimp and crab are found in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, the catching of these species would be confined entirely to Canadian fishermen if the gulf area were classed as Canada's territorial waters under the terms of Bill S-17.
When the minister is investigating the possibility of securing new markets for all the species of fish caught by Canadian fishermen, I suggest he also inquire about the possibility of selling all of the scallop. The part we use, the muscle, is only a fraction of the total scallop, all of which is edible. In fact in Europe the greatest delicacy is the scallop roe and other parts of the scallop.
We must also carry out further investigations on behalf of our lobster fishermen. This year lobster fishermen are suffering from a small catch in almost every area along the

DEBATES	January 25. 1966
eastern coast. Some of the fishermen believe this is due to the fact that foreign trawlers are catching the seed stock of large lobsters on our offshore banks. Draggers from New Bedford landed over $1 million worth of offshore lobsters from the Georges bank area last year, and we have no record of the quantities taken by the huge Russian fleet operating in this area.
There seems, Mr. Speaker, to be no scientific data as to whether our inshore lobster population has any connection with the population on Georges bank. I therefore suggest to the government that they set up a joint Canadian-United States commission to get at the biological facts and, if necessary, attempt to get agreement on the need for preserving the large lobsters on our offshore banks through the international commission for North Atlantic fisheries. The Russians cooperated this summer in that they allowed United States observers to go on their ships, and they might well co-operate in this instance also.
The world today is searching with increasing anxiety for food for its growing population, while our major scientists in Canada and the United States seem more concerned with the type and quantity of minerals to be found on the moon. I believe we should adopt a series of priorities in our research and do first things first. If the Minister of Fisheries and this government will follow some of the suggestions I have proposed for the fishing industry, they will accomplish three things. There will be less need for catch insurance, there will be more income and a higher standard of living for our fishermen, plus more food for the world's growing population.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a new member speaking for the first time in this house I am under no delusions that this house awaits my words with bated breath. However, I do feel very privileged and honoured to be able to speak in this chamber, the walls of which have echoed with the great voices of the past. I am still in a state of semi-shock as I wander about corridors frantically searching for officers or officials and trying to untangle the great web of rules and procedure. I suggest that lectures be given new members, and in addition that a committee be formed specifically to assist new members in launching their parliamentary careers. I think if this is done it will enable all of us to take our places in this house with greater facility and ease.
January 25, 1966	COMMONS
Now, Mr. Speaker, I come from Lindsay, Ontario, which is rampant with Toryism. Eventually I settled in the riding of Welland, which was so ably represented by Dr. McMillan for 15 years. Affectionately known as "Doc", all members of this house respected and loved this man. I think at this time the house should pay tribute to his memory, and we all join in wishing him and his wife the very best indeed.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext:
As a member, Dr. McMillan worked hard for his constituents. Bereft of all flamboyance, artifice or sham, he never covered the walls of this house with purple prose. Though gentle in manner, he had a tough, inquiring mind and made his presence felt by the reasoned content of his argument. As a member of the Liberal caucus his common sense and quiet wisdom influenced many decisions. Prudence prevailed when Dr. McMillan spoke. As a family man of unblemished character, absolute fairness, devoid of devious ways, false pride, pomp or circumstance, he personified all that is worth while in public life.
In paying tribute to a man who brought dignity to this chamber, and was a fine representative in the best traditions of the house, I do so with a purpose. His example and code of conduct can be a shining beacon to all of us. Personally I will endeavour to emulate this man who graced the House of Commons for years and embodied to a marked degree all that is good in public affairs; gentility of spirit, a real concern for people, complete honesty and quiet dedication.
Physically, Welland riding is urban and rural, including three chief population centres; the town of Thorold, the city of Port Col-borne and the city of Welland. It should be noted that we have the newest city in the Dominion of Canada in Port Colborne, which achieved city status on January 1, 1966. Situated at the entrance to the Welland canal, the city of Port Colborne with a long and honoured past can look forward as a new city with pride and purpose to a glowing and prosperous future. I am sure all hon. members will join with me in wishing this newest city the very best in the years that lie ahead.
The most striking physical feature of our riding is the Welland canal, part of the St. Lawrence seaway. This canal bisects the city of Port Colborne, the city of Welland and the town of Thorold. From an aesthetic and tourist viewpoint it is attractive to have ships from all parts of the world gliding through 23033-15
DEBATES	225
The Address-Mr. Tolmie the centre of your city. In fact we claim a unique breed. We claim a breed of "ship watchers". However, on the other hand the inability to traverse our cities when canal bridges are raised has inflicted grevious economic and traffic hardship.
Shortly after my election, like a veritable bolt from the blue, it was announced by the Minister of Transport that over 4,000 acres of land had been expropriated immediately to the east of Welland for a possible new canal bypass. This would have the effect in one fell swoop of taking the Welland canal out of the city of Welland and placing it elsewhere. The new canal bypass would be about eight miles long, cost around $110 million and take about six years to build.
The extreme need for this bypass is obvious to anyone familiar with the Welland canal and aware of the ever increasing, gigantic shipping traffic.. In Welland, with the delay of many bridges and the tortuous channel, the canal is a bottleneck impeding ship traffic throughout the entire seaway, with a resultant debilitating effect on our entire Canadian economy. By building this canal bypass bridges will be eliminated, wind protection afforded ships and a straighter and wider channel provided, all factors leading to the seaway's essential purpose, the easier, safer, and faster passage of ships.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
If we as Canadians wish to meet the increasing demands of ship traffic; if we wish to see western wheat sale commitments met, directly benefiting the prairie farmer and indirectly helping our entire Canadian economy; if we wish to thwart the challenge of the Americans building a competing canal, then all logic and economic sense dictates that we start this Welland canal bypass immediately.
For Welland itself a canal bypass is the answer to our prayers. The nightmare of traffic congestion will fade away, and Welland can plan its future growth properly and economically. The possibilities for the old canal site fire the imagination. Boating facilities, park areas, dock areas could be made available. An inland harbour, a little Antwerp on the Niagara peninsula is not a wild dream. What city in Canada has a landlocked lake in its very centre, resplendent and glowing with fantastic opportunities for unlimited development?
At this point I inject a sobering note. At the present time, although the land is expropriated, the government has not made a decision as to whether the canal bypass should be
January 25, 1966

The Address-Mr. Tolmie proceeded with. It is of the utmost importance to Welland to know as soon as possible whether the bypass is going to be built. We are in an intolerable situation now. Commerce and business cannot make decisions as to future growth; proposed highways are left in abeyance; expropriated home owners cannot decide to move or stay; construction of a proposed tunnel under the present canal, essential to the very welfare of Welland, will be delayed. In sum Welland, hanging in a state of suspended animation, most anxiously awaits a decision. I am confident that the government, itself faced with much investigation before decision, as its past record indicates will deal with this matter with dispatch and efficiency. May I say that the seaway authority and its officials charged with this matter are an effective and dedicated body which with unfailing courtesy discharge their many duties.
Mr. Speaker, legislation is sometimes passed without any evidence of direct or indirect benefit to the economy. I state categorically that the Canada-U.S. automotive agreement has within a few months of its passage brought increased prosperity and employment to Welland. From my own personal knowledge two plants have expanded as a direct result of this most enlightened piece of legislation. I know that the benefit felt in Welland reflects in only a small way the tremendous success of this auto pact. No doubt these encouraging results will mean the possibility of similar policies in other spheres of our economy.
It should be noted that Lake Erie borders my riding, and the general problem of pollution of the great lakes is convincingly illustrated in this area. Suffice it to say that large sections of Lake Erie are dead, their waters unable to sustain fish life. The shores of Lake Erie are increasingly deluged with evil smelling algae, destroying property value and depriving the people of our area of the right to enjoy some of the greatest sand beaches in the world. The eradication of this menace to our greatest natural resource is a municipal, provincial, federal and international responsibility. Steps have been taken to prevent this pollution, but greater measures are needed.
I mention the problem of pollution of our great lakes to alert members to this insidious danger, so that all parties can acquaint themselves with the background of this situation and in later discussions make contributions to its solution.

Culturally, Welland riding is blessed with people from every racial background, giving us a vibrancy and uniqueness which we deeply cherish. Here the fact is well demonstrated that people though different in origin are the same in their needs and aspirations and can live in peace and harmony, ennobling and enriching themselves and their community.
We are fortunate to have many French speaking people in our area, and at this time in our country's history when words such as extremism, separatism and special status are bandied about, I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadians of French extraction in our area reject all clarion fanatic calls to national, historic pride of race or culture. Their wants are simple and legitimate; to be treated as equals; to be accepted as Canadians; to be allowed in dignity to infuse their heritage into the happy blend of polyglot races which adorn our ridings, whose only desire is to move forward together in a common bond of humanity.
May this great nation of ours, fraught with the perils of colossal geographical distance, threatened with the divisive forces inherent in any country with different tongues and traditions, look upon the happy intermingling of people in our area and be reassured that it is possible to live in co-operative harmony and good will.
To achieve greater mutual acceptance and unity between the two founding races the barrier of foreign language must be erased. Our common goal should be to provide for every boy and girl in this nation the rare privilege and distinction of speaking both the English and French languages.
Mr. Speaker, briefly in relation to immigration policy, I believe there is much scope for the clarification and liberalization of policies which have existed for a number of years. At a time in our history when we have the space, when the booming economy requires additional manpower, it would seem logical that increased immigration on a broader basis is not only justified but necessary. I am pleased to see that our government, aware of these factors, is considering immigration policy and will be laying proposals before parliament.
Mr. Speaker, as a new member I am proud to be now part of a crew that has sailed the ship of state through troubled waters to achieve great and lasting reforms; to mention a few, our Canada Pension Plan, the most imaginative and humanitarian piece of legislation ever enacted by mankind; the birth of
January 25. 1966

a new flag; the first federal minimum wage law; the new concept of the U.S.-Canadian automotive trade agreement.
More must be done, much more. From the inexhaustible wealth of this happy land, casting aside petty politics and bickering, we must wrest from the very bowels of this country the means to nourish and foster even greater social reforms such as medicare; greater educational assistance; help for the unfortunate in all spheres of human endeavour. What we have done to date is only the symbol of things to come, only the dawn of a new era of compassionate legislation ministering to the real needs of our peoples.
I say that not one member can rest when in this nation one child wants; not one member can rest when one child suffers from intolerance, bigotry or discrimination; not one member can rest when through suspicion and ignorance forces are at work tearing away the fabric of our constitution and gnawing away the bonds of unity.
Mr. Speaker, as a new member I do not presume to lecture this house. Perhaps I am undergoing an agonizing appraisal of my own worth. I only hope I have enough of that most highly prized, that most rare and precious commodity, courage, to adhere to my principles and make some real contribution to our national life.
I end as I started, Mr. Speaker. In this house, which you so graciously adorn, proud and humble I take my place.
At one o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 2.30 p.m.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should first like to congratulate you on your election to the high office which you hold and which I know you will fill quite capably. I should also like to congratulate the mover and seconder of the Address In Reply to the Speech from the Throne, the hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Goyer) and the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury). They are both to be congratulated for the contributions they have made to this debate.
I myself welcome the opportunity to take part in this debate because we find Canada at the crossroads of so many important things that what we do today will, I feel, have a tremendous bearing on Canada's future. It pleases me a great deal, indeed I feel humble, to come back again to Ottawa and try to contribute something to the future growth of Canada.
The Address-Mr. J. H. Horner
Many have called the Speech from the Throne a warm-up of a bunch of leftovers and really that is what it is. Nowhere does it face the basic issues confronting Canada today. No mention is made in it about the cost of living index which has gone up 10 points in the last three years, a tremendous increase of over three points each year. Whom does this affect? It affects those who are on a stationary income that does not increase with the cost of living. Many of these people are retired. They are living on pensions and nothing has been done to compensate them for this sharp increase in the cost of living index. To me this is a gross error. I am pleased to support the amendment before the house, which will be voted on this evening, because I believe it is a worth-while one and the people concerned are in need of what it seeks.
In the Throne Speech we are told that parliament will be judged by its actions rather than its words, but if that speech indicates anything at all it indicates that we are going to have a whole lot of words and very little action. Our old age pensioners are in need of assistance. The Speech from the Throne completely ignores them. Though it goes on to speak about poverty and aid to those in need, nowhere does it outline any concrete steps which will provide aid for anything. It is interesting at this time, shortly after a general election, to note whether or not some of the election promises are contained in the Speech from the Throne. It is also interesting to note how the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) voted in the house the other night compared to what he said during the election campaign. As far back as 1958 the party to which he belongs promised to increase old age pensions to $100 per month but the other night in the house he voted against providing any additional assistance to our senior citizens. I trust that he will prove his intentions tonight by action rather than by words.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
The hon. member to whom I referred also stated during the last election campaign that some people believed there was a tremendous vacuum building up in the country which would suck him into the office of Canada's Prime Minister. Some of the stuff-I use that word advisedly-that is being peddled around Alberta during election campaigns is absolutely amazing, particularly when compared with what one hears the same people say in Ottawa. This is a serious situation and we
228	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. J. H. Horner should all be judged by our actions rather than by our words. I am certain the hon. member lor Red Deer will be judged in that way in the next election, whenever it may be, by the people in the province of Alberta. One cannot continue to advocate one thing and vote against it here in Ottawa.
In looking at the Speech from the Throne I also considered it with interest in respect of the aid that will be forthcoming to the agricultural industry. In looking now at the agricultural portfolio I am seriously concerned. Let the Liberals travel throughout western Canada to ascertain what is wrong with the agricultural industry in that area, let them make repeated trips over long distances; I am sure they will in the end find that the difficulty so far as the agricultural industry is concerned has arisen because this government has never considered that industry to have any priority or rank.
Let us consider the poor former Minister of Agriculture from Calgary. He was a fine gentleman who worked hard for the industry but received little or no co-operation from his colleagues. The farmers of western Canada sensed this situation very quickly. The difficulties were obvious to everyone in view of several things that happened, one of which was the removal of part of that individual's portfolio for a period of one month followed by its return after bitter criticism levelled by his predecessor. These things convinced the farmers in western Canada how slight was the concern of the rest of the Liberals with regard to the agricultural industry.
At this time the agricultural industry employs somewhere in the neighbourhood of 11 per cent of the population and contributes over 40 per cent of the gross national product. This is a prime industry in Canada which should not be bandied about in the way it has been in the past. Basically the industry is proud of the way the new minister is attempting to do his job but again he is receiving stiff opposition from his colleagues in the government. We hope he is allowed to do his job and we stand behind him, but how is he to win his battles against the increasing odds? The government has split the agricultural portfolio in three ways. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) is still in the game because the wheat board, according to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp), still reports to the Department of Trade and Commerce. The Minister of Finance still keeps in contact with the wheat board, according to what was reported in the Swift Current Sun of January 14, 1966, which is not

DEBATES	January 25, 1966
long ago. According to that press report the the Minister of Finance said:
As Finance Minister, I now will not be responsible for or to the wheat board.
Surely that is a surprising statement in view of the fact that we thought all along he was responsible. He continued and said:
However, I will answer for the wheat board in the house at the new session of parliament, and hope to remain a useful contact with them for the government,-
What kind of a slaughter is this? I suggest it is an example of the old rule of divide and conquer applied to the agriculture department. What has happened? We had a minister who had strong influence in the government. He made his presence felt and brought about beneficial results to the whole agricultural industry of Canada. What has this government now done? I am afraid they have picked the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. Greene) as the next goat. The former minister was a hard-working member but he was the goat of the twenty sixth parliament. Will the present Minister of Agriculture be the goat of the twenty seventh parliament?
The present government has divided the Department of Agriculture and taken away a good deal of the responsibility from the new minister. Some of that responsibility has been given to the Minister of Trade and Commerce who, if we believe what is said in the newspapers, is a very able man, perhaps intended to be the next Prime Minister of Canada or at least the next leader of the Liberal Party. That hon. gentleman is not allowed even to speak for his department. The Minister of Finance is the speaker in this house so far as wheat board policy is concerned. This is again an example of the rule of divide and conquer.
We now have a Department of Forestry associated in some way with rural development. That fact points out that the minister holding that portfolio will also have tremendous influence on the agricultural industry. In view of these facts, what are the government's plans for the hon. member for Renfrew South? Surely he is expected to catch the hot potatoes and attempt to throw them back at someone else.
The attitude now taken by the Liberal government in respect of agriculture reflects the Liberal attitude over the years. Even under the Mackenzie King regime the Liberals followed the rule of divide and conquer because it is safer for everyone in that no one knows what is being done or who is responsible. This practice has worked effectively in
January 25, 1966	COMMONS
the case of the C.B.C. I suppose the Liberals have decided to adopt it on behalf of other government departments.
We come to this house at this time not knowing who is responsible for national parks, and I suspect there is so much confusion that not even the members on the government front benches know who is responsible. The situation is the same in respect of agriculture and I know that the farmers all across Canada take a dim view of it. They would rather see one strong man than four weak ones fighting among themselves without any influence in the government. We saw a good example of this inefficiency recently in respect of the transportation of grain. When the situation was brought to light the Minister of Finance met with the Minister of Agriculture and the C.P.R. The two ministers came out of that meeting with very different statements and views. It is obvious to anyone who has read the newspapers since that meeting that the Minister of Agriculture is engaged in a series of conflicts with the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the spokesman for his department, the Minister of Finance.
The Minister of Agriculture is apparently involved in conflicts with many of his colleagues in the cabinet. We hope he is the successful one and we are behind him because he has struck at one of the roots of the problems now existing in western Canada. I refer to the inefficient transportation of grain.
I remember the former Minister of Finance stating in his first budget speech that huge sales of grain had been made to communist countries and that they had been the lifesav-er with regard to the balance of payments problem in this country. What is going to happen today to the industry which has pulled Canada out of its balance of payment problems in the past? Surely there is some doubt about the answer in view of the fact that those responsible are fighting among themselves rather than co-operating in an attempt to solve these problems.
What happened at the meeting a day or two ago to which I referred? Apparently the Minister of Agriculture was told that the situation was not the C.P.R.'s fault and that the C.P.R. was doing a tremendous job. The Minister of Finance came out of the meeting and said the whole situation was the fault of the operators at the Vancouver terminal. If anyone cares to read the Calgary Herald of last Friday, he will see there a sharp denial by
DEBATES	229
The Address-Mr. J. H. Horner the Vancouver terminal operators. That article states that the Vancouver port operators deny that any delay was caused by them in respect of grain movement. The article states that sharp protests were sent to the Minister of Finance and that the Vancouver Merchants Exchange, representing the whole coastal operation, stated that the facilities were operating at about half capacity because of the lack of grain. The article also states that the United Grain Growers said that their terminal is half empty and has been half empty since the middle of November.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
What is the existing problem? The difficult situation which now exists has resulted from the shortage of box cars and the inefficiency of the railways in the movement of grain. For the life of me I cannot understand why the Minister of Finance does not say to the railways: Get this grain moving, because the agricultural industry has helped the Canadian economy in the past and will continue to do so in the future. But no. He takes a dog in the manger attitude toward western farmers generally and says, You are well enough off and we will move your grain when we want to. This is the attitude taken by a former Minister of Trade and Commerce, C. D. Howe. We told him to go out and sell Canadian wheat because there was a market for it in the world and he made that famous statement, "If they want to buy it, let them come and get it". A similar attitude was taken by C. D. Howe's deputy minister when he said: "The grain is there. We will get it to the ports eventually. Abide with us." This is what the farmers are being told and it is not good enough.
Many farms in my area are on a one bushel quota. Not too far away the farmers who are on a C.N.R. line are on a six bushel quota. Many farmers in my constituency have been able to move only 20 per cent of their grain although over 50 per cent of the crop year has already passed. You can imagine the rushed and confused state those points will be in during the last two months of the grain year.
This attitude of saying continually that everything is fine, the grain will move, is not good enough. We believe that the Minister of Agriculture is right when he says there should be an investigation into this whole question. The port facilities and the operations of the wheat board have not been investigated at all in the past few years. Until a few years ago the annual report of the
230	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. J. H. Horner wheat board was put before the Agricultural Committee every year but since this government took office they have not given the elected representatives of the people the chance to examine the operations of the board and see how it is handling this commodity. The wheat board should be brought before the agriculture committee. The C.P.R. should be brought before the Transportation Committee. The reports of these two bodies should be fully investigated in order that we may know why box cars have not been available and grain has not been moved.
We should examine statements like that of the United Grain Growers that terminal elevators in Vancouver with a capacity of 3J million bushels have been half empty since November. Surely we should examine these matters and see where the problem is, so that in the years ahead we may benefit from the mistakes that have been made in the past year. The U.G.G. went on to say that they can handle 480 box cars a week and they have only been getting about 270. The port facilities at Vancouver can handle something like 30 million bushels a month but they have only been getting something like 14.7 million bushels a month for the past while.
Where is the problem? It is not, as the Minister of Finance says it is, at the terminals and in the port facilities. It is not at the country elevators because I know the farmers are ready to fill them the minute space is available. Therefore the problem must lie between the elevators and the ports in the transportation field. It is said that the Crowsnest pass rates are perhaps not compensatory and maybe this is so. We in western Canada believe that they are. They are the Magna Carta of western Canada and they will be maintained. But other costs have gone up. We do not doubt for one minute that railroading costs have gone up in the past few years, but what steps have the railways taken to become more efficient in the handling of grain?
Recently we have seen new box cars come into being for the handling of pulp chips and for the transportation of automobiles. But wheat is still transported in the old 2,000 bushel cars. In the movement of wheat there has really been no change. With the use of aluminum alloys in box cars there is no doubt whatever that greater efficiency could be achieved in the handling of this commodity if there was. a desire to serve. The Minister
