of Agriculture put his finger on the problem the other day. Greater efficiency could be achieved if there was on the part of the C.P.R. the desire to serve and to meet their obligations to Canada, because we all know that the C.P.R. has received compensation far and beyond the services they will be able to provide. This compensation has taken the form of grants of land, mineral rights and so on in western Canada.
To my mind this is a very serious problem, and in the days ahead I hope the cabinet can get together and iron out who is the boss. Does the Minister of Trade and Commerce need the Minister of Finance to be his spokesman? Does the Minister of Agriculture have any influence at all on his colleagues in the cabinet? This is what western Canada will be watching. They will be watching the Minister of Agriculture, not because he is an easterner, not because he is a lawyer, but to see if he can produce the goods and exert any influence at all on his fellow cabinet members. We will be watching him carefully. I am aware of the small measures for agriculture mentioned in the Speech from the Throne: Another 5 per cent on the premium for crop insurance, a national dairy commission, a feed grain marketing agency which will have the power to buy, store and sell. We will be watching these measures too. But the best thing the Minister of Agriculture can do right now for western Canada is move the grain and we hope that he will be successful in this connection. I should like to deal with another subject that is very important in western Canada today. I refer to our relations with other trading nations. Over the week end I had the opportunity to visit the site of Expo '67 and see the preparatory work being carried out there for Canada's centennial and Expo. I was greatly impressed with the groundwork that has been done. We were told that it is on schedule and I hope it is. I know this exposition will be of tremendous benefit to all Canada. I was a little disappointed though, to put it mildly, that on the map showing where the pavilions are to be built by the various countries there were the words "Republic of China" with an arrow running down to a little square box. One would naturally think that this referred to communist China. At least, that is what my knowledge would lead me to believe. But no, it refers to Formosa.
When I questioned one of the officials I was told that invitations were sent out by the
January 25, 1966

Department of External Affairs and no invitation had been sent to communist China. I think this is a grave omission. Canada, a young nation, had an opportunity to invite these people to our trade fair and try to convince them that capitalism and communism can co-exist. This is where the complete hope for world survival lies, in the fact that we must convince communist China that we can live alongside them without fighting with them. Russia under Khrushchev reached this degree of education or civilization, however you want to term it. Russia under Khrushchev realized that she must co-exist with other nations, and said that she could co-exist with them.
China has to be brought along in the same way and to the same degree through education and civilization. How better could Canada play a major part in bringing about co-existence than by inviting China to take part in our trade fair? We have apparently invited Russia, and Yugoslavia. Russia is going to spend $15 million to build their pavil-lion at the Canadian Exposition. Russia and Yugoslavia are communist countries; yet we did not invite communist China. One of the authorities in Montreal said to me-he kind of smiled when he said it-"Which would you rather have, the United States or communist China?" To my mind this was just an empty threat. I am certain that in this case the government is using the United States as a goat because they do not have the intestinal fortitude to be bold, to take the initiative and invite communist China.
The United States was not particularly happy when we continued to trade with Cuba a few years ago. The late President Kennedy was smoking a Cuban cigar but when this was pointed out to him he quickly threw the cigar away. We continued to trade with Cuba. We then started to trade with communist China. The United States was not particularly happy when we traded with Russia. Wheat surpluses started to disappear in this country and in the United States because of our extensive trade with communist countries. We have relieved the wheat surplus of the world to the point where there is almost an equal balance. There is a manageable balance in this commodity at the moment.
The United States was not particularly happy with the steps we took but we proved to them that these steps were in the right direction and they are now trading to some extent with Russia and trying to sell them wheat. There was a golden opportunity and

The Address-Mr. J. H. Horner still is for the Department of External Affairs to send an invitation to communist China. We have traded over a billion dollars worth of goods with them in the past three years. Why can we not invite these people to attend a trade fair? Do we not believe that trade is a two way street, that we must buy from them if we expect them to continue buying our products in the quantities in which they have bought them? We must make overtures to them far greater than we have in the past.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
I believe there is still time for the Secretary of State for External Affairs to act in this regard. We are a young and growing country that cannot continue to turn a blind eye to one of our greatest customers, a country with a quarter of the world's population. In my opinion the steps that should be taken are grave and the people of western Canada are watching with interest the government's attitude toward this particular question. Government officials really do not have to take so many trips to the west to ascertain what is wrong. They must know they failed to act during the last three years and that this is what is wrong. If they fail again they can expect little support at the polls in the years ahead.
I have one other recommendation to make with regard to agriculture generally. We all know that the costs of production in the field of agriculture have been rising. One of the first statements that the Minister of Agriculture made after assuming office was that the family farm must be protected. This is an old cliche that farm leaders trot out every once in a while. We will watch what action he is going to take to protect the Canadian family farm.
In 1949, 23 per cent of the price of a loaf of bread went back to the farmer. Today, something less than 7 per cent or 8 per cent of the price of a loaf of bread goes back to the farmer. In 1949 the beef price index stood at 100. In 1965 it was 140 but there was no real change in the price the farmer received for his livestock when he sold it to the packing plant. We say that there must be greater efficiency in the agricultural industry including greater efficiency by farmers. The Speech from the Throne indicates that the government intends to buy uneconomic units and replace inefficient farmers with efficient farmers, men who know how to operate farms. Let them try to buy up the people who are marketing the farmers' goods because in this area lies the greatest inefficiency.
January 25, 1966

The Address-Hon. Paul Martin
The Price Spreads Commission reported that in 1959 wholesalers' profits were around 15 per cent. They have gone up to nearly 25 per cent today. This represents a 25 per cent profit on the marketing of the farmers' goods. Yet we wonder why there is such a spread between what the farmer receives and what the customer has to pay for these products. This is where the greatest percentage of the difference lies.
We look at the farmers' cost picture. We can look at the whole list and find, according to a recent article in the Family Herald, that in the last ten years the costs of equipment and material have gone up over 20 per cent, that farm wages have gone up over 50 per cent in the last ten years and the cost of fertilizer has gone up over 25 per cent. Gasoline, taxes and all other costs have increased. Yet there has been no real increase in the return to the farmers from the sale of their products. Then we say to ourselves. Is the farmer efficient? He must be tremendously efficient in order to stay afloat. In my opinion this is the problem.
In an earlier speech in this house I suggested that there should be a thorough investigation, a continuation of the work of the Price Spreads Commission. I am certain that the inefficiency in the marketing of the farmers' products is one of the real causes of hardship for many of the farmers. I will continue to watch the legislation which is introduced in the house in the hope that it will meet some of the problems facing agriculture today and in the years ahead. Certainly the Speech from the Throne contains no prediction that any really helpful legislation will be introduced in so far as Canadian agriculture is concerned.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first of all extend to the Speaker of the house my warmest congratulations on his unanimous election to the high office which has been entrusted to him. To you, Mr. Deputy Speaker, I likewise say how proud we are that the members of this house has selected you to associate yourself in a collaborative way with Mr. Speaker. Perhaps as the member of this house who has been here longest I may be permitted to extend special congratulations to the mover (Mr. Goyer) and seconder (Mr. Stanbury) of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, both of whom acquitted themselves with distinction.
I trust, sir, that there will be an opportunity soon for the house to undertake a broad

review of foreign affairs. Today I thought I should like to confine my statement on behalf of the government, to the crucial issue of Viet Nam. No issue has so much preoccupied public opinion in Canada or the members of this house in recent months. No issue has aroused greater misgivings or greater uncertainty about where the right course for Canada lies. Probably no issue has cast a darker shadow on the prospects of peaceful accommodation and peaceful co-operation in the world.
The policy of the government in relation to the Viet Nam problem is now a matter of record. It was stated before the External Affairs Committee on Wednesday and Thursday, June 9 and 10. If I restate it today, it is because I regard it as right to do so at the outset of this new parliament and in the light of recent significant developments in the situation.
In our view the situation in Viet Nam needs to be viewed from three separate perspectives. First, there is what I might call the perspective of internal dissent in South Viet Nam. This is something we must expect in any new country where the people live on the margin of subsistence. It exists because the process of social and economic transformation that is the basis of any significant development is bound to involve dislocation and disruption. It exists in greater degree in a country like South Viet Nam because of the intervention from the outside. This in turn has made it impossible for successive governments in that country to lay a recognizable basis for political stability.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
But let us not on that account equate that outside intervention with the desire for social and economic change. Let us remember that long before the conflict in South Viet Nam erupted into open hostilities it was the agents of change-the administrators, the teachers, the public health workers and others like them-who were the prime targets of terror. Let us remember that whatever the change of government in Saigon, and there have been many, the level of that terror did not abate. And let us also remember that when the government of President Diem was forcibly overthrown in 1963, it was not overthrown by men or groups whose loyalty was pledged to the Viet Cong.
This is not to discount or to downgrade the hold which the Viet Cong has by one means or another been able to establish over sections of South Viet Nam and its people; it is merely to suggest that we would be entirely
January 25, 1966	COMMONS
mistaken if we regarded the Viet Cong as embodying a consensus of dissent in Viet Nam. So far as we know, none of the major groupings in South Viet Nam, the Buddhists, the Catholics, the trade unions, the intellectuals, the students, are significantly represented in the Viet Cong movement. Certainly there is nothing to suggest that there is any basis for the claim of the Viet Cong to be the sole legitimate representative of the people of South Viet Nam.
Second, there is the matter of outside intervention. Admittedly this is a difficult situation to disentangle in a divided country. After all, it is often argued: What is the sense in speaking of intervention in a context where Vietnamese are involved on both sides? I suggest to the house that whatever the circumstances in which these dividing lines were drawn they have come to reflect political realities which it will take time to alter. They neither justify nor diminish the fact of aggression.
What is happening in Viet Nam may not be aggression in the classical sense of the term but it is aggression all the same, and it is aggression carried out in this case under the guise of a war of liberation. The aim of that aggression is to establish in South Viet Nam a form of political organization which we have no evidence to suggest that the people of South Viet Nam would freely choose for themselves.
We have said that in principle we appreciate and support the purposes and objectives of the policy of the United States. This was affirmed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) when the matter was first discussed in this house. We have said that because, as the Prime Minister put it, we cannot in this nuclear world of ours "afford any permissible kinds of international violence" of the kind by which the North Vietnamese are trying to achieve their objectives in the South. We have said this because we are of the view that the people of South Viet Nam must be left to work out their own future free from outside pressure or intervention. We are not disposed to deny to the people of the south the right of self-determination which we have conceded to others in accordance with the solemn principles of the charter of the United Nations.
Third, there is an even more broad perspective, one from which I think the course of developments in Viet Nam has to be viewed.
I do not want to urge on the house the "domino" or any other currently fashionable 2303a-16
DEBATES	233
The Address-Hon. Paul Martin theory. But I do suggest to the house that we cannot look at the situation in Viet Nam in isolation. In neighbouring Laos the country is to all intents and purposes partitioned. The part that is under Pathet Lao control is being freely used for the movement of men and materials from North to South Viet Nam. Members of the armed forces of North Viet Nam have been engaged in open attacks against the armed forces of the royal government of Laos. All this is in clear contravention of the undertakings solemnly given in Geneva in 1962; and Canada was a member of that conference.
In northeastern and southern Thailand there are the beginnings of the same kind of terror which marked the first phase of insurgency in South Viet Nam. As in the case of South Viet Nam this is being aided and abetted from outside but with this difference, that the Thai Patriotic Front, as it is called, is still operating from Peking. It has within the past several weeks been joined by a new clandestine organization, the National Liberation League and Army of Malaysia, which is dedicated to the overthrow by revolutionary means of the government of Malaysia.
Are we, then, seriously to assume that all these movements are coming into being because the legitimate channels of local dissent in these countries have been closed? Or is this part of the pattern of permanent revolution which is being propagated in some quarters? I suggest to the house, on my responsibility as Secretary of State for External Affairs, that these are questions which we must seriously ponder before we condemn United States policy in Viet Nam in the very vigorous terms used by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) in his earlier intervention in this debate.
That is our assessment of the forces that are at work in the present conflict. There are those who would have us alter that assessment for the mere sake of giving the appearance of Canadian independence as though independence consisted only in taking positions which are necessarily against those of one's friends. Our policy in this situation represents our own honest assessment of the position and is not a reflection in any way of pressure imposed on us by the United States or by any other country. In this matter we are as independent as is Her Majesty's Government in the United Kingdom. I say to the house that after more than 11 years of active involvement in the situation in Viet Nam we
January 25, 1966

The Address-Hon. Paul Martin are perfectly capable of arriving at an independent assessment of that situation without having recouse to false credentials. The question we must surely ask ourselves is this: Can we ignore the challenge of the aggression by these communist liberation fronts in Asia?
Were we able to ignore the situation in Europe 20 years ago? I am not saying that the situation in Europe now is comparable with that existing at present in Asia. Undoubtedly there is a detente in effect between the west and the Soviet union in Europe. I am talking about the situation in Asia where a different state of affairs prevails, but where there are some comparisons to the history of the immediate post-war period in Europe. No one will deny that mistakes have been made in Asia and I think some have been made by the United States. But there is, it seems to me, a parallel between the situation in Asia and that in Europe following the end of the war.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
We must ask ourselves what the failure of United States efforts in Asia would mean to us as well as to that country. We must ask ourselves what it would mean to India, to Thailand, to the island countries, the Philippines, New Zealand and Australia. We must ask ourselves what it would mean to many countries in Asia and Africa which, although critical of the United States, would be deeply concerned over a communist victory in Viet Nam. I ask what would be the concern of the Soviet union in these circumstances. I must ask the house whether Canada's real interests would be promoted by a United States defeat. I must ask the house what such a defeat would mean by way of encouragement to an aggressive brand of political action. It is because of these considerations for Canada and other countries that we cannot deny the importance of this conflict in Viet Nam to us all. I have given the house my assessment of the conflict. I shall now turn to the policy which we have thought it right for Canada to follow in relation to this conflict.
In the first place, there is our membership on the International Commission. The house is well aware that this has been an increasingly frustrating commitment. The circumstances facing the Commission today bear little resemblance to those envisaged when the Commission was given its mandate. Nevertheless, we have throught it right to maintain a Canadian presence in Viet Nam. We


have done so because the Commission still has a function to perform in bringing its objective judgment to bear on the facts of the situation, because the Commission continues to maintain, at least in symbolic form, the validity of the Geneva Agreements on which, all the parties seem to agree, any fresh settlement of the Viet Nam conflict must be constructed, and because the Commission may still be able to play a part in the context of such a settlement, if not to serve as a channel of contact between the parties themselves.
The charge is sometimes made that Canada has failed to act impartially in discharging its responsibilities on the Commission. This charge, in my judgment and on my examination and on the advice of my officers in whom I have the fullest confidence, men who have served Canada in Indo-China for 11 years, has no basis in fact. I reject it without any hesitation. We have acted impartially in relation to all the facts and all the evidence which has come before the Commission. Contrary to what is sometimes asserted, we have been associated with findings against South Viet Nam as we have been associated with findings against the North. We subscribed to the Commission's Special Report of June 1962 because it represented a balanced presentation of events in Viet Nam. We also appended a minority report to the Commission's special message of February 1965, not because we disputed the findings of the majority, but because it was our view that there were other factors which it was legitimate to include on the basis of all the evidence available to us at that time. In all this, I think, we need make no apology to our Commission partners for the way in which we have interpreted our responsibilities on the Commission.
To my knowledge, for example-and I state this not by way of criticism but by way of fact-our Polish colleagues on the Commission have never found occasion to support a finding against North Viet Nam and have frequently refused even to participate in an investigation where such a finding was likely to be the outcome. Yet it would be found that Canada as a member of the Commission did not hesitate where this was called for to criticize the actions of the government in the South. The Commission has no authority to criticize any state not a signatory of the Geneva agreement but the implications are there for everyone to read and there was no reservation made in the Canadian position with regard to the Commission's report of 1962.
January 25, 1966	COMMONS
Then there is the matter of sending Canadian troops to Viet Nam. We have made it as clear as it can be made that we would not regard such a course as being compatible with our responsibilities on the International Commission in Viet Nam. This is far from being the frivolous argument as some have professed it to be. The Geneva cease fire agreement which the Commission is there to administer prohibits in its very terms the introduction of military forces into either part of Viet Nam. It would scarcely be right for one of the powers which has been entrusted with the supervision of the agreement to abet one of the parties in an infraction of its terms. Any other position on our part would certainly have the gravest consequences to our ability to carry out peacekeeping functions not only in this area but more generally and in other contexts. I believe we can all take pride in Canada's achievements in this field of international activity and I believe it is imperative in the interests of international peacekeeping not to jeopardize our ability to contribute significantly to such activities.
Altogether apart from membership on the Commission, however, the government's policy, as I have stated it twice in this house and as it was reaffirmed by the Prime Minister the other day, is that the government has no intention to recommend at any time the commitment of our forces to Asia unless pursuant to an obligation under the charter of the United Nations.

No, I do not think it is.
My next point is this. Our policy has been directed toward helping to bring the present conflict from the battlefield to the negotiating table. This has always been our position and it remains our objective. We have made it clear, and the Prime Minister did so again only the other day, that we do not look upon the present conflict as being amenable to a military solution alone. We have taken every opportunity available to us to probe the possibilities for peace and, indeed, we are doing that at this very time. We proposed a pause in the bombing of North Viet Nam last April, not because we looked to one side only to make concessions but because we hoped that such a pause might provide a climate in which it would prove easier for the other side
23033-16J
DEBATES	235
The Address-Hon. Paul Martin to respond in a positive way. We have welcomed the current pause, which has now been in effect for an entire month, and the search for a peaceful conclusion of the conflict which has accompanied it. Although the absence of any positive response from the other side has been a matter of deep disappointment to us, we have expressed the hope that the pause might be further extended until all reasonable possibilities have been exhausted. I simply ask: Have all reasonable possibilities been exhausted? I would hope that the pause would continue as long as possible. I would hope that before any final step were taken in this regard the most careful consideration would be given to an examination of any indication that North Viet Nam was now seriously engaged in examining the possibility of negotiations. In the final analysis, however, we must recognize that it is not for Canada to take the crucial decisions which lie immediately ahead since we are not a party to the hostilities. On the other hand, we do think there may well be a contribution which Canada can make to an ultimate settlement because of the long experience we have had of the problems at issue in this whole area.
We have expressed our regret that in a situation which so deeply engages the concern of the international community, the United Nations has been prevented from playing any effective part. We recognize, as the Secretary General did again in his press conference on Thursday last, that there are reasons why the United Nations has been unable to act in the present circumstances.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)

speechtext: Because it has been ignored.

speechtext:
My hon. friend is quite right; it has been ignored. It is clear that China would regard the Secretary General, I regret to say, as persona non grata. It is true that China is not a member of the United Nations. It is true that South and North Viet Nam are not members. It has not been possible to use the United Nations fully and there has been a failure on the part of some nations to appreciate the great role that the office of the Secretary General affords in so delicate a situation.
These are obvious reasons why the United Nations has been unable to act and why the Secretary General himself has not been able to act as fully as he would have liked. But I hope he will continue to explore all the
238	COMMONS
The Address-Hon. Paul Martin possibilities that may be open to him as Secretary General to encourage action that will set this conflict on a course of peace. I would also hope with him that there may yet be a role for the United Nations in securing the terms of any settlement of the present conflict. If and when that time comes, I can assure the Secretary General and the house that the Canadian government will do whatever it can to enable the United Nations to carry out its responsibilities in this area as it has done in similar circumstances elsewhere.
We have also directed our thinking toward the great task of rehabilitation in that whole area that will have to form a part of any durable settlement of the Viet Nam conflict. We have resumed our pledge to participate in the works of the Mekong development committee. We have subscribed to the capital of the Asian Development Bank which has now been established. We are prepared to devote further substantial resources to regional development in Southeast Asia in which I hope both communities in Viet Nam eoukl play their full part and derive their full benefit. Indeed, I would go further and say that I would look toward this whole field of regional development as providing a framework within which these two communities might be able to establish a basis for mutual acceptance and co-operation.
Over the past month, Mr. Speaker, efforts have been made by many countries to explore the opportunities there may be for peace in Viet Nam. Canada alone, and Canada in concert with others, has done what it could do to try and bring about negotiations. The house will be aware of the efforts which have recently been made by the United States to reaffirm its readiness to negotiate an honourable conclusion to the present conflict. We are satisfied beyond any doubt that the efforts of the United States during the past month through its Secretary of State, through its Vice President, through its delegate to the United Nations and through others, have been sincerely directed toward trying to bring about negotiations without any preconditions. It is regrettable that no response has been forthcoming, and I think it is only fair to point out that, whatever some may think of the course of action by our neighbour, the fact is that no one can suggest that the United States has not sincerely sought to achieve negotiations. The result has been a massive and continuing shortage of housing in the centre of the city for newcomers and people of low income.
I will not take the time of the house on this occasion to review the housing statistics in detail. It is sufficient to say that they are shocking. Considering the amount of housing required, the statistics reveal an almost complete failure to provide public housing in the

All responsible people who have studied the problem agree on the pressing need for thousands of new housing units in Toronto. They also agree they cannot be provided profitably by private industry. In this wealthy country we may be reluctant to admit this fact but the truth is clear. We do need public housing in great quantity for our low income urban families and we need it quickly. Over the years the demand has been building up steadily. In proportion to need Canada has less public housing than any other civilized country in the western world.

That corporation has performed well the job entrusted to it by parliament. However, it holds firmly to the belief that its function is essentially that of a friendly banker charged with the responsibility for financing housing construction and urban renewal. It does not accept direct responsibility for providing the public housing which is required in our cities. Its view is that this is a welfare function and is no part of the function of any banker, friendly or otherwise.

I believe this is a very, very important item, not because the University of Western Ontario is located in London, not because it is generally recognized, I am sure, by everybody here and throughout this country as being the finest university in Canada-

Mr. Speaker, when we recessed for dinner I was speaking on the subject of education. I cannot help going back to the election campaign of 1963 when the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) promised some 10,000 scholarships. I believe the total cost was to run in the neighbourhood of $10 million. This promise of course never did come to fruition. Instead we did receive legislation setting up the student loan fund. I am wondering why this promise was swept under the rug. The student loans make it very difficult for a young man getting out of university because he is saddled with a great debt which he has to pay and upon which he has to pay interest. Perhaps this scheme did serve a purpose, but there was a great deal of propaganda about it.
It is my understanding we are going to expend roughly $40 million for scholarships now. This, of course, is four times as much as the promised expenditure on scholarships in 1963. If we receive this amount on a pro rata basis in the same manner as we received the promised amount in 1963, we should receive four times as much. Four times nothing, of course, still remains nothing. I am just wondering if this promise will be forgotten, as so many other promises have been from time to

time. I feel we should have some action in this field. This is something that is very necessary, very worth while. I feel the government should honour the promises they made during the recent election campaign.
Another subject I am rather duty bound to mention in this house is that of job training. We have either to train these people in some skills, or fail to keep pace with the new era of automation into which we have already entered. Either we equip these people to live with some semblance of dignity and selfrespect or we will have to look after them through some of our social services.
This training program would have a tendency to make these people become good citizens. Otherwise they will just become charges upon their own municipalities, as well as the provincial and federal governments. I say that this is a must program. According to the press a statement was made here in September that the immigration department was desirous of bringing into Canada some 180,000 skilled workers. Immigration is very important, but I should like to ask this question: What about our own Canadians? I feel we ought to think that charity generally begins at home, and that it is our responsibility to help every individual fill a worth-while job. I know that when I make this statement I am speaking for every person in this house, regardless of party, somehow or other we must do something to protect the dignity of the individual.
I had intended to speak at great length on the subject of trade and commerce. Yesterday the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Hees) mentioned several of the subjects I had in mind. If I were to recapitulate those things it would be redundant. However, there are one or two subjects upon which I must touch. He spoke rather briefly of the balance of payments, and of the shortcomings of our Department of Trade and Commerce. He mentioned that this year total imports might be something in the neighbourhood of $1 billion over exports. I must refer to an item that appeared in the London Free Press on September 4, 1965. The heading on this article reads, "Imports up 16.4 per cent in June". This article states:
Imports rose in June this year to $798,600,000, up 16.4 per cent from the June, 1964 total of $686 million, the Dominion Bureau of Statistics reports.
Farther along in this article I read:
The bureau reported earlier that exports in June foil 7.4 per cent from June, 1964 to $737,200,000.
January 25, 1966

With regard to our exports to Great Britain the article reports:
Exports fell 11.9 per cent in the month to $99,300,000.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this is a very serious picture. I am just wondering if perhaps there is something wrong with our general economy. What is the answer? Is this one of the reasons an election was called? Is there something wrong internally with our economy about which we should know? Certainly the signs are here.
In 1962 the government, then the official opposition, blasted us because of the devaluation of the Canadian dollar. However, they have not seen fit to change it. I am just wondering if a further devaluation is the answer to our problem. I think this is something that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) along with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) might seriously consider. Should we drop the value of the dollar to the 90 cent level? These are very important times, very serious times in this country of ours.
I must say something once again, Mr. Speaker, with regard to the retarded people, and not just retarded children, in relation to our present immigration laws. I knew of an individual in this country who received an offer of a much better position in the United States. He went to the southern United States, arranged for the rental of a home and moved his furniture. When he went to cross the border the officials refused permission for his 20 year old son to enter the country. I made it my business to meet this boy. He is mildly retarded, having an I.Q. of approximately 60 to 70. He did go through grade 6. In my estimation he was a nice lad and he does perform a daily labouring task. This was a great privation for this particular family and I believe that something should be done about our immigration laws, and in a fashion which would be reciprocal with the United States, to meet situations of this kind.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
I believe a bill was recently introduced into Congress to amend their laws, and I feel that a similar bill should be introduced here. But I should like to see such a bill come from the government side of the house, because it would have a much greater chance of passing in that event than if it were to be introduced in the form of a private member's bill. However, I propose to introduce such a bill, but I should like not to get credit for the bill. I should like to see the people who need it get the credit.
23033-17J
The Address-Mr. Irvine
I must make reference, Mr. Speaker, to a meeting which I attended in July of this year of the Association of Retarded Children. We who have been fortunate and who have families which are not mentally retarded should be very happy to come to the aid of others less fortunate, because mental retardation could happen in any family. This meeting, attended by Congressman John Fogarty of Rhode Island, was held in the Royal York hotel, Toronto. We discussed many of these aspects, and I am now going to quote one of the items in a brochure which was presented at that time. According to section 5 of the Canada Immigration Act of 1952, the following are prohibited entry to Canada as immigrants or as visitors: Persons who (1) are idiots, imbeciles or morons; (2) are insane or have been insane; (3) have constitutional psychopathic personalities; and (4) are afflicted with epilepsy. Whatever the original intent of this act it is now out of date both in its implications and in the very language it employs.
The words "idiot", "imbecile" and "moron" have not been found in modern medical literature for many years. They are considered repulsive as well as outdated. The same can be said of the word "insane"; and medicine has yet to define the word "psychopathic".
There are many other cases than the one I cited, Mr. Speaker. Many are related in this brochure which I am sure everyone in this house should read. One short item in the brochure makes this whole act, I think, ridiculous. It says:
Our records contain the case of a retarded boy whose mother attempted to take him to New York state on urgent business of her own. When she discovered that the boy would be refused she made arrangements for his care and attempted to continue her journey alone. She also was refused admission as "an alien accompanying an inad-missable alien".
I am very much concerned over these people, Mr. Speaker. It is a matter which should be corrected, and corrected immediately or as soon as we can make the necessary arrangements with the United States immigration department. If there is worry that these children or grown up people would become charges either on a state or on this country at some future time, then I should like to suggest that should those born in Canada become charges on the state of their choice then they would be our responsibility. And, vice-versa,, those coming from the United States to Canada would be the charges of their respective states from which they happened'
January 25, 1966

The Address-Mr. Irvine to come. I say that because of the great number who would come here compared with the number who would go to the United States.
I must say something with regard to the small businessman who, at one time, was considered the backbone of this great country of ours. The small businessman, however, is getting smaller all the time. Some of them are even going out of business, as evidenced by the great number of bankruptcies we have had. The large ones are getting larger. For the independent businessman the cost of doing business with our high cost of living, which has gone up 15 points over the last three years, makes survival difficult. There is also the cost of administration of such things as deductions which employers make on behalf of their employees. Other matters are income tax and unemployment insurance, federal matters for which they receive no compensation for work done. Such things as compensation for employees and sales tax are provincial matters, but certainly income tax is a federal matter, as is unemployment insurance and deductions under the Canada Pension Plan. As I say, these employers receive no compensation for doing this work.
I have here an item from the Toronto Daily Star for January 3 in which the following appeared:
Employers were taking a hard look at employee payroll deductions as the Canada Pension Plan came into effect. With nine deductions from a pay cheque not uncommon, the administration cost of mandatory deductions has become more than just a nuisance to industry.
Further on in the article this statement appears:
M. M. Dillon Ltd. of London, Ont., an engineering firm with about 235 employees, will go to payroll data processing to help cope with the paper work.
"We felt that the inception of the Canada Pension Plan would be a good time to swing over to data processing," said W. G. M. Wilson, personnel manager for Dillon.
Usual payroll deductions here are Ontario hospital, income tax, unemployment insurance, pension plan, medical insurance, salary continuation insurance and voluntary group life insurance."
These are matters with which they are faced, Mr. Speaker.
One big company has indicated that their administration cost in connection with these matters was about 1 per cent of their gross income. This being a large firm with some 900 employees, it is quite easy to see that the cost to a smaller firm with 10, 20 or 30 employees might well run to 3 per cent, which might represent its total net profit.


I have a note here which I received from the Canadian Tax Foundation. Provision for remuneration is made provincially in many cases. In British Columbia it is 3 per cent on the first $2,500 and then 1 per cent. In Saskatchewan it is 3 per cent on the first $600 and then 2 per cent. In Ontario it is one half to 4 per cent with a 50 cents minimum. In Quebec it is 2 per cent, and in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland it is 3 per cent.
I should like to ask what we are going to do to assist these people, because something must be done. Some of these firms find they must hire somebody, a man or a lady, simply to look after this particular procedure alone as far as the firm is concerned. In many cases if these returns are filed late there is a penalty. If there is an overpayment it is not always refunded, which I think is grossly unfair. These employers should receive something by way of remuneration for the bookkeeping services which they are doing for us.
I also object, Mr. Speaker, to another matter of grave importance. Just before the recent election campaign, ads appeared in many papers across Canada in connection with the Canada pension plan. A beautiful picture was drawn depicting someone working in a mine, and the ad stated how much he was going to pay into the plan and how much he would receive at age 65. But there was confusion; it was confused with the old age security plan in that the two items were added together. However, that is not the point I am making. Think of the number of papers in which these ads were run.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
I do not know whether the party in power would want us to think that public money was used for election purposes. But, Mr. Speaker, it would look like it. Let us consider for a moment the amount of money which was spent in advertising redistribution across this country. In the Toronto Daily Star on June 15, 1965, there were ten pages of advertising at approximately $1,000 a page-$10,000 in one paper on one day. These advertisements were run in every paper of any size right across Canada-maybe on not quite so many pages; I did not check all the papers. But if one multiplies the cost of this one insertion by hundreds the total figure runs into hundreds of thousands of dollars, possibly into millions.
Why? Was this running an election campaign on public money? Was this a softening
January 25, 1966

up process intended to make the news media sympathetic? If not, why was it done just before a federal election?
It is all over now. We have had that election. The people have spoken. But the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) is reported to have said in September, 1965, that if he did not have a majority he did not want to form a government. He also said, I understand, that if there was no majority there would be an election within six months. Today I am wondering just what his intentions are.
He is further reported to have said in regard to the old age security payment that it would be raised to $100 a month, or even more for those who were in need. I am led to assume by this that he meant a means test. I know this was mentioned this afternoon by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) but I have to admire the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Brown) because he has a conscience and because he wants to serve the people according to the dictates of that conscience. I congratulate him for having placed notice of motion number 50 on our order paper. I should like to say that this hon. member is a good friend of mine.
I should also like to say this that there is no suggestion in the amendment before us that this money should be taken from the Canada Pension Plan. It was mentioned incidentally by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) that this is a possible source, but the amendment itself contains no suggestion that this money should come from the pension plan. On this basis I feel the hon. member for Brantford should be able to vote according to the dictates of his conscience. I hope his notice of motion indicates that on the government side of the house there is to be a free vote on this issue. It would be refreshingly new and different if there were. It is time hon. members opposite considered their position closely before casting their votes tonight. Would it not be an excellent thing if we could all get together and make this a unanimous decision?
Judging from the notices of motions on the order paper, if members opposite do not agree to it now, they intend to bring in this increase later, anyway. Would it not be an odd coincidence if this were to happen just before another election, always supposing of course they have notice that another election is coming.
Where do we go from here? The Prime Minister told us that he did not want to form a government unless he had a majority. Then
The Address-Mr. Guay he made the other statement I have already mentioned. Is the right hon. gentleman prepared to resign? We are waiting for him. Does he want us to form a government? We are waiting for that, too: We can do it. Does he want another election?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following several of my colleagues who made their contribution to this debate, I am pleased to congratulate you and the Deputy Speaker of this house upon your election to those respective offices. I also congratulate the mover and the seconder for performing their duty with so much eloquence and ease.
My speech will deal mainly with one particular paragraph of the speech from the throne, as reported on page 8 of Hansard of January 18, 1966, and I quote:
My government will propose a vigorous program, in co-operation with the provinces, to foster the training of workers and to assist in bringing into productive employment those who are now unemployed or inadequately employed. You will be asked to consider a measure to improve the system of training allowances provided under federal-provincial agreements.
Mr. Speaker, here are the main problems that must be dealt with regarding poverty. First of all, ways must be found to offer at all times a sufficient number of jobs to those who are prepared and able to work and then to make sure that all citizens are qualified to take advantage of available jobs.
Although many other problems must be solved, if we want to avoid poverty, we must create enough jobs for all our able-bodied citizens.
Today, full employment is the main goal of most countries. In Canada, since the end of the war the government has been openly pursuing that goal.
Full employment, as it is generally understood, does not guarantee prosperity or satisfactory living standards for all. This well-known fact has now become for the community an increasing worry.

January 25, 1966
The Address-Mr. Guay
It is felt that full employment has been reached when 97 per cent of the labour force is working. However, that average can be reached even if there is a higher proportion of unemployed in some age groups, in some localities and in some periods of the year.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Last summer less than 3 per cent of our labour force was unemployed, and this, for the first time in almost ten years. Even then, unemployment was higher, namely 4 per cent, in the province of Quebec and in the Atlantic region, and possibly two or three times higher in certain areas; the rate was 6.4 per cent for the 15- to 19-year age group, 8.1 per cent for labourers and 5.5 per cent in the building industry. A full employment policy must be concerned not only with the number of jobs but also with the distribution of these jobs.
Mr. Speaker, such a policy must also take into account the quality or the productivity of the jobs, i.e. the case of the worker who, although he works full time, earns an insufficient income.
In rural areas this problem gave rise to suggestions likely to increase agricultural production, to foster rural development and the merging of marginal farms. In urban centres, traditional solutions shaped themselves into minimum wages and other labour standards. More recently the emphasis has been put to a greater extent on the research of incentives that will provide employment in secondary industries located in areas where the percentage of unemployed is greater.
The most serious problems caused by poverty can be found in groups of people cut off from the labour market. I am thinking of pensioners, persons lacking in vocational training, school drop-outs and problem-ridden families.
Steady periods of full employment would alleviate the economic problems facing those people, but the real solution would be to provide funds to promote the interest, the education and the professional guidance of the small wage earners and their children so that they become more efficient, more independent and get higher wages through their own efforts. The problem in establishing a policy regarding those people, is to set up assistance programs to encourage their quest for independence, while protecting their income and preserving their dignity.
Poverty appears in many guises, but the most usual and surest test is the amount of cash income.

A method of determining the spread of poverty would be to draw a dividing line of poverty, and then figure out, for instance, the number of unmarried persons earning less than $1,500; the number of married couples with an income below $2,500; the number of four member families with a income inferior to $3,000, and so on. This calculation would help measure the true difference between an adequate income and the actual one. For many reasons, however, such a calculation is not enough to lay down a government policy. First of all, the actual income index does not take into account a number of factors affecting the welfare of the family, such as income in kind, fringe benefits, property ownership or tenancy, food requirements of workers doing different types of work, and so on.
In other words, income may be an incomplete or biased indication of poverty. Second, poverty is not an absolute condition in itself. As Galbraith said "People feel destitute when their income, even if it is sufficient as a means of livelihood, is markedly lower than that of people around them." This would lead us to believe that income in relation to the community average would make a better index.
Third, knowledge limited to income levels is not a sufficient basis to establish a plan. The cause of low income must be sought to formulate certain policies such as for instance, unemployment insurance, winter works programs, manpower mobility programs.
For other types of programs, such as old age pensions and unemployment assistance, it is essential that we know the particular features of low income brackets. Therefore, in addition to the breakdown of income, it is necessary to determine various complementary aspects of poverty, such as unemployment of rural and urban workers, the degree of education of the unemployed, the extent to which health and housing have affected education and employment, etc.
Mr. Speaker, considering underemployment, the number of unemployed people in a country does not alone give the exact picture of poverty or of a lack of manpower utilization. In a way, it is a matter of definition.
On the one hand, official unemployment statistics disregard the unemployed who may want to work but cannot for physical or psychological reasons. On the other hand, these figures do not take into account those who work but do not earn enough to provide a decent standard of living for their families.
January 25, 1966
These people are usually classified with the inadequately employed. This category includes people who, through no fault of their own, hold an occasional or part time job, those who have a regular job only during part of the year, and those who are employed all year round but in low production fields. The last are often found in the agriculture and fishing industries.
To achieve a high rate of national growth and have price stability, we must be able to determine, even if only approximately, the labour markets where there are not enough jobs, their geographical distribution and the change in size they might undergo from one period to another. Such information is also important to eliminate poverty.
However, underemployment is a complex phenomenon both hard to define and evaluate, and opinions generally differ on one and the other, except in a very broad sense. Experts brought together by the international labour organization have defined two kinds of underemployment:	visible underemployment,
where you have people who, through no fault of their own, have shorter than average working periods. Hidden underemployment, that is what we have where full time workers earn abnormally low wages or else where jobs do not allow them the fullest use of their capabilities or knowledge. Satisfactory means have yet to be found to evaluate this last category of underemployment. Low income has been chosen as a determining factor, because underemployment is one of its main causes, although, admittedly, not the only one.
Using what figures are available, the extent of the obvious underemployment in Canada may be arrived at through various methods. The decennial census is the most detailed source of information on underemployment during part of the year, for it gives information on the apportionment of salaries earned in various jobs during the year under review.
In 1961, 3.6 million male wage earners declared how their income was distributed during the year preceding the census. Of these, 2.8 million worked for 40 weeks and 2.7 million of them averaged more than 35 hours a week. This means that no more than three quarters of all male wage earners in Canada worked full time the whole year through. One quarter of all wage earners,
780.000,	worked for less than nine months,
460.000,	for less than six, and almost 200,000 worked for less than three months.
Mr. Speaker, according to the census definition of a family, 23 per cent of all Canadian
The Address-Mr. Guay families earned less than $3,000 in 1961. Of those whose breadwinner is a woman, more than half earned less than $3,000 and two fifths earned less than $2,000. Three out of every five families living on fishing, one out of every two families living on woodcutting or farming, and one labourer out of three earned less than $3,000.
[DOT] (8:40 p.ra.)
Problems with regard to poverty can be subdivided as follows: (1) those of people clearly cut off from the labour market; (2) those of the unemployed; (3) those of people whose present production is too low to provide an adequate family income.
The first group includes retired people, widowed people with dependant children, permanently handicapped people and others who cannot possibly be on the labour market. The solution to be adopted towards this group is to set up assistance programs providing adequate help and ensuring that their dignity be respected, while continuing to promote some sort of independence wherever possible.
The group of the unemployed is extremely diversified. On the whole, seasonal variations of activities account for roughly one third of the unemployment. In many areas, it is the main cause of poverty.
The hardest unemployment problems to solve include those concerning handicapped persons at the occupational level and school drop-outs. The unemployment rate among workers under 20 is more than double the national average. But, proportionately speaking, even if the unemployed are less numerous among older workers, they are more likely to suffer longer from unemployment once they lose a job.
Included in the third group are people affected by underemployment. Those are the persons working less than they would like to at part time or casual jobs or jobs with a low return or income. In this sense underemployment forms an important part of the problem of poverty and especially rural poverty.
Unemployment and underemployment are problems which must be considered in the context of a society whose industrial and employment structures are now undergoing rapid changes. That evolution calls for greater adaptability on the part of the labour force. The distribution of jobs has changed and more and more jobs require better training. Technological changes are now happening at such a rate that many workers will have to get additional training several times to fill new jobs.



January 25, 1966
The Address-Mr. Guay
Under the present circumstances a manpower program directed toward a high level of employment and a highly productive economy requires such things as increased mobility, effective training methods, youth orientation, services to foster a desire for accomplishment and regional development programs.
Those are the very measures that must be adopted to solve the particular problems resulting from poverty. In other words, a great number of programs needed to alleviate poverty must not be concerned exclusively with low income people. They must also apply to the labour force in general.
Mr. Speaker, to consider various solutions, I refer to the newspaper Le Soleil, of June 11, 1965, and I quote an article entitled "Jean Marchand opens up."
The President of the C.N.T.U. deplores the lack of an employment program. According to him, man's right to work is not recognized under our economic system. In his opinion, that right has become a commodity, submitted in that respect to the law of supply and demand, a situation which is unacceptable because it destroys the worker's personality. There is no doubt, he added, that through their sustained efforts, labour unions have forced the enactment of legislation to correct the immediate results of unemployment, although full employment is not considered by most North American economists as a goal to strive for and attain. The solution to the employment problem, according to Mr. Marchand, is economic; the right to work cannot be respected unless new jobs are created as a matter of deliberate policy. He stated that that is all the more imperative and urgent that the progress of productivity or even automation tend to reduce the amount of human labour needed for a given production.
The distribution of the working population between the various sectors of economic activity is not unalterable, but subject to changes which result mostly from technical progress and productivity; fewer people are employed in primary industries and agriculture; then the number of people employed in secondary industries increases, steadies down and decreases; and, finally, the number of jobs in the third sector increases very rapidly. Such trends seem to be the general law and any realistic employment program must accept it as such.
Mr. Marchand goes farther than that.
According to him, efforts to maintain the present spread of employment would be to no avail. When the number of jobs is cut down to reduce production costs, the steps taken for this purpose are even desirable, provided the workers involved are sure to find suitable employment enabling them to keep up their standard of living. For Mr. Marchand, such a program would imply concerted action in the various sectors of the economy, a collective effort to cover manpower reconversion costs or create new jobs in depressed areas.

Second, I would like to quote from the same newspaper and the same series of articles by Mr. Roland Parenteau who said;
The need for increased participation of the state in the economic and social life of the province is a fact recognized by everybody.
He does not mean, however, that the state must assume all responsibilities. The state, as such, is suited to assume certain responsibilities; in other fields, it is better to leave things to private enterprise.
The main responsibility of the state, according to Mr. Parenteau, is to draw up the master plan. This does not mean, however, that the state should not call upon the services of representatives of private enterprise. But once this plan is drawn up and duties have been assigned to everyone, it can be said then that the greater part of the work of the state is done. The latter does not have to substitute itself to individuals.
Mr. Parenteau concludes that the state will more readily accept the role of co-ordinator and referee when it is itself relieved of the production and distribution of this wealth.
Then, said Mr. Parenteau, we do not forget, in the province of Quebec, that one of the objects of planning is to bring about a better geographical balance.
During the federal-provincial conference of last July, the federal government emphasized not only the necessity of increasing training but also the necessity of carrying out thorough research in the field of training needs and the problems of motivation, in order to contribute to the development of more efficient techniques for adult education. It was suggested, then agreed in principle, to set up a number of special pilot projects which would serve as a practical and thorough investigation on the best means to meet the training needs of adults, especially those who have been unemployed for long periods of time or who have been engaged in activities of a low productive nature.
The results of such an experience and test will be of practical value not only in the areas concerned but in all parts of the country and in all provinces. We all recognize, I think, the need for greatly increased adult training- We all know that the problems and needs of such training are of a special nature and differ greatly and in many respects from the problems of education at the school level. We still have a lot to learn on means to ensure its efficiency. That will be the usefulness of the pilot projects.
January 25, 1966

The federal proposals were more thoroughly discussed last September, at a meeting of federal officials and representatives of the Canadian Education Association and of the Canadian Association of Administrators of Labour Legislation.
At the time, the minister said:
The revised proposal which resulted from that meeting is the first item on today's agenda and the main reason for this meeting.
Those pilot projects are a preliminary and necessary step of this major effort for adult training which, I feel, is one of the main elements of manpower policies in Canada.
I am convinced that one of the most important jobs for the government today is to give leadership in the development of our manpower resources. I use the word "government" on purpose. I do not mean the federal or provincial government. I mean both together. It is only through co-operation that we will be able to meet the needs of those that such governments have a responsibility to serve.
I noted with pleasure that, in its second report, the Economic Council of Canada strongly supported our viewpoint concerning the vital importance of a manpower policy. Our human resources are the key to economic progress and sustained prosperity, and the full development of our human resources calls for high levels of education and training, and also first class employment services.
The tasks, both immediate and future, are manifold. The present lack of skilled manpower must be filled, partly through immigration, but mostly by training further the workers which we already have. We must see that available skills are used at the right time and at the right place. We must take new steps to lessen useless seasonal unemployment and eliminate pockets of underemployed manpower. But above all we must bend our efforts toward raising the level of practical knowledge of those who have left school and who make up the present or the potential working force.
The Economic Council has pointed out that in spite of the greatly increased opportunities for technical training open in the last few years to students in vocational training schools, "no marked progress has been made in the training or re-education of the present labour force".
For adult training to be truly successful, techniques are needed, and the required techniques are neither known nor tested enough. We must study them and adopt special schemes to make training more acceptable to adults; we must find new ways of increasing motivation in the individual and improving community attitude toward training. To ensure the success of training, there must be a general feeling that the adult who attends a training school is not retrograding but that, on the contrary, he is actively engaged in living, that what he is doing is normal, productive, in a buoyant economy.

I should also like to congratulate the mover of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne-unfortunately I am not able to address the hon. member in his native language-who confronted us so well with the issues that face him from his own particular viewpoint. I congratulate, also, the seconder of this motion, the hon. member who spoke to us of his constituency and his dreams in such an eloquent manner.
I should like to spend a few moments, if I may, in dealing with some aspects of this most recent in a series of Speeches from the Throne. One of the things that it speaks of in a variety of different ways is the question of poverty. Recently we had emanating from one of the many federal-provincial conferences the enunciation that there is to be a poverty line of some $3,000, I believe it is, for a family of a husband, wife and two children.
I only wish that an average yearly income of $3,000 was enjoyed by the people of Prince Edward Island, for if this figure is to be taken as any kind of an average, we in my province do not nearly measure up to even what is called the poverty line. It is important to me that great, worth-while and effective steps be taken by the house to deal with this serious question of poverty as it expresses itself in many different forms across this country.
January 25, 1966

The Address-Mr. David MacDonald
I can speak very feelingly on this question because I think in large measure I am here in the house this evening because I have been sent here by people who through personal experience and association are deeply concerned with poverty. They know the face of poverty well, and many of them have worn this face for an extremely long time.
On of the things that interests me greatly in the Speech from the Throne, is the suggestion that there will be a review of the tax structure and a reconsideration of the fiscal relationships between the federal government and the provincial governments, for on this question hangs a great deal of the hope, or lack of it, in the province of Prince Edward Island. As is well known through the many statistics that are published from time to time, we in Prince Edward Island have a very low standard of living. This is expressed in a number of ways. One way, of course, is the number of people who emigrate frequently from Prince Edward Island. It is also expressed in the continual story of chronic unemployment, low education standards, and so on.
Year after year we have our provincial ministers-and this has been true no matter which party they have represented-coming to Ottawa to ask for some kind of adjustment, in light of this serious situation. It was one of the important achievements of the previous administration in this house that great things began to happen not only for Prince Edward Island but the maritimes, and the special needs of the maritimes region were finally taken into account.

It is somewhat tragic that since 1963 we have seen a loss of interest in this most vital problem. Maybe it is true, as one person remarked recently somewhat facetiously, that we should start our own kind of separatism down in Prince Edward Island. Perhaps we should think of joining the "Boston States". Whether or not the answer does go back to the proposition that we would have been better off in union with the New England seaboard and that great area known as Megopolis, I am not sure; but I do know there is a tremendous economic discrepancy between much of the maritimes region and the so-called heartland of Canada wherein we are situated at the present moment.
We must begin to deal with the needs that exist in this particular area and we must deal

with them realistically. It is not enough for a federal authority to just recognize the needs of a province and its population; other things must be taken into account as well. You must remember that the province of Prince Edward Island must maintain a full provincial government and civil service to administer a population not much larger than that of a small city. There are special expenses that must be met if the province is to maintain its own identity.
One must realize the educational needs which we must provide. If we are to overcome this serious situation, we must provide teachers and the proper support for educational institutions that are not at the average or below average, but are above average.
I found it interesting to learn that Prince county has one of the highest proportions of people of school age of any geographic area in Canada. Some 47 per cent of our population in Prince county is under the age of 19 and is thus eligible for some kind of academic training. I was glad to see mention made in the Speech from the Throne of some kind of training allowance being made available to those who are past school age and wish to further their education.
We have been quite willing year after year to spend money for certain kinds of welfare and unemployment insurance. We must be willing to invest heavily in the field of supporting adults in their 40's, 50's and, yes, even their 60's while they seek to obtain an education they were unable to get during their school years.
When one considers the matter of agriculture and fisheries in this Speech from the Throne, really much more is said about agriculture than one could almost expect, and you are inclined to suspect a guilt complex was at work here because so little has taken place in this field during the last two and a half years.

Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the right hon. Prime Minister for having again lead the Liberal party to victory. I also congratulate from the bottom of my heart my constituents from Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm for having sent a Liberal to parliament. I hope we will have from now on, many years of prosperity, social security, industrial, agricultural and tourist development in this beautiful region on the north shore of the St. Lawrence.
The riding of Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm will be represented in Ottawa with dignity, clear-headedness and drive.

Mr. Speaker, hon. members, this is the new voice of Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm. All my life I wanted and I tried to be a builder in the largest sense of the word, and I think I have succeeded in becoming one. In my riding of Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm I have built houses by the hundreds, schools, public and industrial buildings, sewers, water mains, streets, roads, and I have contributed to many other plans of public and civic movements. To achieve all of this I had very limited means of action, so it took a lot of work, courage and ambition. If today I am in federal politics it is because I think it is the strongest lever I can use to continue in my endeavour to help as much as I can to build a better Canada for all Canadians and for all French Canadians.
The duty of all of us here is to keep Canada united and to assure equal partnership to English Canadians and French Canadians, the two founding races of our country. For this we must succeed in making each and every Canadian feel secure and at home anywhere in Canada, and especially here in Ottawa.

Mr. Speaker, many hon. members have heard speeches in the past about the constituency of Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, but I should like to give a brief account of this county as seen through the eyes of a new

The Address-Mr. Comtois member. My constituency is about 210 miles long, about 36 miles wide and encompasses more than 7,500 square miles. On the southern side it is bordered by the St. Lawrence River and on the northern side by the county of Abitibi. The county of Berthier bounds it on the eastern side and the county of Terrebonne on the western side. There are over 51 municipalities spread out over this huge territory which has a population of more than
135,000	people. Within its boundaries can be found a great number of rivers, and a still greater number of lakes, mountains, an abundance of natural resources and landscapes of a rare beauty. The people are hardworking, intelligent and courageous.
You will understand, Mr. Speaker, that in such a riding the needs are many. Allow me to name a few that I should like my government to take into consideration.
The riding of Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm is made up of three very distinct areas: a tourist area in the north, a farming area in the centre and an industrial and residential area in the south.
I would be very happy if highway 18 were considered as an access road to the tourist area of unequaled beauty to the north of St. Donat de Montcalm, which would become a real paradise for the people of the Montreal area.
In addition, the building of a dam at St. Donat de Montcalm, between Lake Ar-chambault and lake Ouareau, would allow pleasure boating on a huge inland body of water.
I commend my government for including in the speech from the throne the proposed establishment of a fund for financing major rural developments projects and agricultural rehabilitation, as well as for other measures to raise and protect farm incomes in order to ensure adequate incomes to our farmers.
I hope this parliament will enable eastern farmers, particularly those in my riding, to benefit from crop insurance, from the Canadian dairy commission and from the livestock feed grain agency.
I shall do my utmost, Mr. Speaker, to attract small or secondary industry to our area specially to those where they are most needed to balance the economy.
Therefore, I hope that the regions of Re-pentigny, L'Epiphanie, L'Assomption, St. Jacques, Rawdon and Joliette will be favoured in the near future.

The Address-Mr. Comtois
The construction of the throughway on the north shore with access roads to L'Epi-phanie, St. Paul l'Ermite and Joliette will be a determining factor in this industrial growth. The construction of the new highway 29 from Ste. Therese to Charlemagne will put my riding directly between the General Motors plant and the steel complex at Becancour, with a link to the north shore through the Trois Rivieres bridge.
I am sure that this industrial growth will be followed by a housing boom, particularly in the region of St. Charles de Lachenaie and St. Henri de Mascouche.
The establishment of the Canada Development Corporation will encourage the birth of new industries and the development of existing industries.
I think it would be quite proper to build a large airport between Joliette and L'Assomp-tion, where the land is well suited. Also, I would like to see the dredging of the Back River and the Thousand Islands River to make them navigable and less polluted; the dredging of the small channel in Repentigny, which is needed from a sanitary, aesthetic and touristic point of view; also, the cleaning up of the mouth of the Assomption river, which has been needed for a number of years.
There is a pressing need of hospitals in Joliette, L'Assomption and Rawdon. New technical schools are also required in that area. A bridge across the St. Lawrence between Sorel and Berthier would be a great economic asset to Joliette-L'Assomption-Mont-calm.
All these needs, and many more, Mr. Speaker, stress the importance of healthy federal-provincial relations, and I am pleased to note that the speech from the throne took this into consideration, in a realistic and intelligent fashion, through legislation intended to encourage job training and increases in training subsidies; legislation ensuring to all Canadians, whether they can afford to pay them or not, all necessary health services; legislation setting up a $500 million fund for health services.
There are still many other projects that could be carried out for the well-being of our people. I shall have the opportunity to come back to this in the house in the near future.
I am convinced that the government will consider seriously the following remarks in the preparation of its budget for the year 1966-67.

After having made a serious study of the finances of this country and the possibilities for additional income, I think the problem of the old age pension increase would be settled if we increase these pensions by $5 a year during five years in order to reach $100 per month by 1970, at which time the eligibility will be reduced to age 65. In this way, as early as 1966, people of 69 and more could get $80 per month and so on until 1970, when they would receive $100 at age 65.
Mr. Speaker, our national pride will be strengthened the day this parliament votes for giving our country a truly national anthem, that is "O Canada".
Our social security system will be improved when this parliament votes for the medicare plan.
The young Canadians who wish to get an education will derive benefit from legislation promoting the expansion of institutions of higher learning, from a national bursaries and scholarships program for students, and from increased financial assistance to universities for the 1966-67 academic year.

In so far as the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury) is concerned, he comes from a riding I had hoped would return one of my former colleagues, a man whose abilities are missed a great deal in this house.
