I wish to extend to the hon. member I have mentioned my congratulations on the method he used and his deportment, in presenting his first speech in this house. This is not the easiest of places in which to speak.
When I say this, a word of caution must be added. In this word of caution I wish to extend my sincere congratulations for the fine example set by the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacDonald) who followed a most commendable practice in that he delivered his speech not from a prepared text but extemporaneously. For a freshman member, this is most commendable.
Hon. members know my view in this regard. I, personally, would banish the use of texts from this house. After all, hon. members have used sufficient eloquence on various political platforms to satisfy the people of their constituencies of their ability to express themselves. So why come to the House of Commons and serve us up with a lengthy speech from a closely prepared text?
It reminds me of an incident of which I read in some book about the British House of Commons. A minister who was not noted for brief speeches or for illuminating speeches entered the house with a whole sheaf of documents. One of the members of the opposition, a leading British parliamentarian of the times, said: "I trust the hon. gentleman will not read us all those documents and bore us with an equally long speech as well." May I therefore commend to the house the salutary example set by the hon. member for Prince this afternoon?
Now, Mr. Speaker, the clock will soon catch up with me as far as the time available for this debate is concerned. I would like to say that I found it somewhat touching the other afternoon to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) spend a great deal of time laboriously talking about the cost of the

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the orders of the day this morning I put a question to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp). My question was in these words: "Now that we have a new parliament and a new Minister of Finance, can we expect action in this session on the matter of increasing the pensions of retired civil servants?" The minister replied with one word, and that one word was, "No". I posted my question for this overtime period tonight because I found that answer of the Minister of Finance a severe shock.
It seems to me that for the .minister to attempt to close off this issue even before this session of parliament gets started is high handed, to say the least. I believe that there are in this House of Commons more members than there have been in any previous house who believe that the pensions of civil servants already retired should be increased. I notice across the way my friend, the hon. member for Victoria, British Columbia (Mr. Groos), who has spoken on this issue and supported our case in previous sessions. I know that the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) has shown an interest in it, as has the

January 25, 1966	COMMONS
hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Chatterton), members to my left in the other two parties, and many members in my own party. I believe there are other members across the way in the minister's party who are interested in the subject. For him to say no, before this issue can be debated at all, is a high handed way of dealing with our retired civil servants.
I do not believe it is necessary for me to spell out the need of retired civil servants, especially those retired some years ago, for an increase in their pensions. The figures which the government brings down from year to year in response to questions I put on the order paper demonstrate this need. I make the point also that the principle of increasing the pensions of persons already in retirement has been established in a good many jurisdictions. Several of the provinces of this country already do it as well as a number of municipalities. My own city of Winnipeg has an arrangement under which the pensions of civic employees already retired can be increased.
I point out also, Mr. Speaker, that we have accepted the principle of escalating pensions that have already been put into effect under the Canada Pension Plan and the Old Age Security Act. In a short period of time these pensions will start to go up if the cost of living index goes up.
I suggest, therefore, that this is a principle that has been established, and that the government could apply this principle to its own retired employees, even as the previous government did in 1959. One of the main arguments that the government uses against this plea is that it has done things for old people generally, that retired civil servants share in those benefits, and that the government, therefore, does not need to do anything further. What the government has done for retired civil servants by increasing old age security pensions from $65 to $75 per month a couple of years ago, what it has done by a number of other measures, was simply a case of doing for them what has been done for everyone. The government has a responsibility to its employees, not just akin to the responsibility it has to all Canadians, but it has a special responsibility as an employer.
Indeed, it has the responsibility to be a good employer. To say that something must not be done for these people because the same things for which we are asking are not
DEBATES	273
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion being done for all other retired employees is to suggest that it would be in order for the government to discriminate against its civil servants in various other ways. This is a doctrine which cannot possibly be substantiated. The government has the responsibility, as I say, not only to be concerned about retired and older people generally, but it has a responsibility to its own former employees, namely the responsibility of an employer.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that despite the cavalier and arrogant way in which the Minister of Finance simply said "No" this morning, this issue is not finished. I believe the members of this House of Commons, even though they did not stay for this debate in the same numbers that were here for the drama of the vote, will not let this session go very far before insisting on a better consideration being given to this matter than that given by the minister on the orders of the day this morning.
Perhaps the whole question can be subjected to further research and divided into its various parts-those who retired a long time ago, those who are retiring at the present time and those retiring in the future. But the issue is a serious one. We in this parliament of Canada are jointly responsible with the government as employers of these people. This is not good enough. I insist that whoever answers for the Minister of Finance tonight in this first overtime period should give a much better answer than the "No" which was given this morning. These people are our responsibility. We have an obligation to them, and there are members of this House of Commons in all parties who are determined to see that that obligation is met.
